cards.q: What is the pinna made of, and why does that structure explain its typical diseases?
cards.a:
• Framework of **elastic cartilage** covered by **perichondrium**, with skin tightly adherent on the anterior (lateral) surface
• Cartilage has **no blood supply of its own** – it is nourished by diffusion from the perichondrium
• The **lobule has no cartilage** (fibro-fatty tissue only)
• So: blood or pus that lifts the perichondrium starves the cartilage → necrosis and deformity; perichondritis characteristically **spares the lobule**
cards.m: Perichondrium = the cartilage's lunchbox: strip it off and the cartilage starves.

cards.q: How are diseases of the pinna classified in this lecture?
cards.a:
• **Infection** – perichondritis, pinna abscess
• **Trauma** – seroma, haematoma
• **Congenital** – e.g. preauricular sinus (also microtia, accessory tags, bat ears)
cards.m: Pinna problems = I-T-C: Infection, Trauma, Congenital.

cards.q: Perichondritis of the pinna: how does it present, what is the usual organism, and how is it treated?
cards.a:
• Hot, red, very tender, swollen pinna; **lobule spared** (no cartilage)
• Often follows **high (cartilage) ear piercing**, trauma, surgery or infected haematoma
• Commonest organism: **Pseudomonas aeruginosa** (also Staph aureus)
• Treatment: **systemic antibiotic** – choose anti-pseudomonal cover, e.g. oral **ciprofloxacin**; admit for IV if severe
• Drain any collection early – untreated it destroys cartilage
cards.m: Pierced cartilage + Pseudomonas → Perichondritis → give Cipro. Lobule spared = no cartilage to infect.

cards.q: How do you manage a pinna abscess?
cards.a:
• **Incision and drainage** of the pus
• **Systemic antibiotic** (anti-staphylococcal and anti-pseudomonal cover)
• Pressure dressing afterwards so the perichondrium re-adheres to the cartilage
• Antibiotics alone are not enough once pus has lifted the perichondrium
cards.m: Where there is pus, let it out.

cards.q: Why does an untreated pinna haematoma lead to a cauliflower ear?
cards.a:
• Blunt trauma (rugby, boxing, wrestling) shears blood vessels → blood collects **between perichondrium and cartilage**
• The cartilage loses its perichondrial blood supply → **avascular necrosis**
• The clot organises and fibroses, and new irregular cartilage forms → crumpled **cauliflower ear**
• The haematoma may also become infected → perichondritis
• Hence it is an **urgent** problem – drain early
cards.m: Blood under the lid starves the cartilage: drain early or it turns into cauliflower.

cards.q: How is a pinna haematoma or seroma managed?
cards.a:
• **Aspirate** the collection (wide-bore needle) and apply **compression**
• **Recurrent** collection → **incision and drainage** with a **button (bolster) stitch** through the pinna to keep the perichondrium pressed to the cartilage
• **Oral antibiotic** cover
• Review in 24-48 h for reaccumulation
cards.m: Drain, then Squash: the bolster stops it refilling.

cards.q: What is a preauricular sinus, where is its opening, and does it need treatment?
cards.a:
• Congenital blind-ending tract from **incomplete fusion of the six hillocks of His** (1st and 2nd branchial arches)
• Pit at the **anterior margin of the ascending limb of the helix**, just in front of the ear; may be bilateral or familial
• Lined by squamous epithelium – may discharge keratin
• **Asymptomatic sinus: no treatment needed**
cards.m: A pit in front of the helix = a fusion fault of the hillocks.

cards.q: How do you manage an infected preauricular sinus, an acute abscess, and recurrent infection?
cards.a:
• **Infection** → antibiotic
• **Preauricular abscess** → **incision and drainage** + antibiotic (do not attempt excision in the acute phase)
• **Recurrent infection** → **excision of the whole sinus tract** once quiet, following its branches down to the **temporalis fascia**
• Incomplete excision is the main cause of recurrence
cards.m: Hot: drain it. Cold and recurrent: cut it all out, down to the fascia.

cards.q: Describe the external auditory canal and explain why furuncles occur only in its outer part.
cards.a:
• About **2.5 cm** long, S-shaped
• **Outer 1/3 cartilaginous**: thick skin with **hair follicles, sebaceous and ceruminous glands**
• **Inner 2/3 bony**: thin skin, no hair or glands, directly on periosteum (very painful when touched)
• Furuncle = infected **hair follicle** → can only arise in the **outer cartilaginous third**
• Wax is made in the outer third – wax deep in the bony canal suggests cotton-bud pushing
cards.m: No hair, no furuncle: boils live only in the hairy outer third.

cards.q: How is impacted ear wax managed?
cards.a:
• Wax is normal and self-cleaning – remove only if symptomatic (blockage, deafness) or the TM must be seen
• **Softening drops** first: olive oil or **sodium bicarbonate** drops for several days
• Then **ear irrigation (syringing)** with water at body temperature (avoids caloric vertigo)
• Or **microsuction** under the microscope, or instrumentation (Jobson Horne probe/wax hook)
• Advise against cotton buds – they push wax deeper
cards.m: Soften, then Shift: drops first, then water or suction.

cards.q: When is ear syringing (irrigation) contraindicated?
cards.a:
• Known or suspected **TM perforation** or history of discharge (risk of middle ear infection)
• **Previous ear surgery** (e.g. mastoid cavity) or **grommet** in place
• **Only-hearing ear**
• **Acute otitis externa** or a painful, inflamed canal
• Hard foreign body (vegetable seeds swell), cleft palate history
• Use **microsuction** instead in these patients
cards.m: Never syringe a Hole, an Operated ear, the Only ear, or an Inflamed canal.

cards.q: What is furunculosis of the ear canal, and what organism causes it?
cards.a:
• Inflammation/infection of a **hair follicle** in the **outer cartilaginous EAC** → **localised abscess**
• Organism: **Staphylococcus aureus**
• Main symptom: **severe pain**, worse on jaw movement and on pulling the pinna
• Localised tender swelling; the rest of the canal and TM are normal
cards.m: A boil in the ear = a Staph boil like anywhere else on hairy skin.

cards.q: How is ear canal furunculosis treated?
cards.a:
• **Analgesia**
• **Oral and/or topical antibiotic** (anti-staphylococcal, e.g. cloxacillin)
• Glycerine-ichthammol wick may be used to reduce swelling
• **Fluctuant** furuncle → **incision and drainage**
• Recurrent furuncles → check **blood glucose** (diabetes)
cards.m: Recurrent boils? Check the sugar.

cards.q: Define otitis externa.
cards.a:
• A.k.a. **swimmer's ear**
• A **generalised (diffuse)** inflammation of the skin of the external auditory canal, characterised by:
• **Oedema**
• **Erythema**
• **Itchy discomfort**
• **Ear discharge**
• Contrast: furunculosis is **localised** to one hair follicle
cards.m: Furuncle = one spot; otitis externa = the whole canal.

cards.q: What are the typical history and examination findings in diffuse otitis externa?
cards.a:
• History: **pain and discharge at the same time**, itch, ± fever, **swimming or ear digging**
• Exam: **tenderness on tragal palpation** (or pulling the pinna)
• **Generalised oedematous, erythematous canal** with pus and debris ± granulation tissue
• **TM intact** (if visible) – helps separate it from discharging otitis media
cards.m: Tragus tender, TM intact = the problem is outside the drum.

cards.q: What are the risk factors for otitis externa?
cards.a:
• **Dermatological**: eczema, **seborrhoeic dermatitis**
• **Allergic**: atopy, non-atopic allergy, sensitivity to topical medicines (e.g. drops)
• **Physiological**: humid environment, immunosuppression
• **Traumatic**: skin maceration (water), ear probing (cotton buds), laceration, radiotherapy
• **Anatomical**: narrow canal (hereditary, iatrogenic, **exostosis**)
cards.m: DAPTA: Dermatological, Allergic, Physiological, Traumatic, Anatomical.

cards.q: Which organisms cause bacterial otitis externa?
cards.a:
• **Pseudomonas species – 50-65%** (commonest)
• Other Gram-negative organisms – 25-35%
• **Staphylococcus aureus** – 15-30%
• Streptococci – 9-15%
• Hence topical drops should cover **Pseudomonas** (e.g. ciprofloxacin or ofloxacin)
cards.m: Swimming pool water loves Pseudomonas.

cards.q: How is otitis externa treated, and when is an ear wick needed?
cards.a:
• **Ear toilet (aural mopping/microsuction)** – drops cannot work on a canal full of debris
• **Topical antibiotic ± steroid drops** (quinolone preferred; avoid aminoglycoside drops if the TM is not seen or is perforated)
• **Ear wick** when the canal is too swollen for drops to enter – drops are placed on the wick, which swells and carries them in; change in 48-72 h
• Analgesia; keep the ear **dry**
• **Severe** (cellulitis, fever, diabetic): add **systemic antibiotic**
• **Ear care** advice to prevent recurrence
cards.m: Clean it, Drop it, Wick it if it's shut, keep it Dry.

cards.q: Otomycosis: organisms, clinical features and treatment?
cards.a:
• Fungal otitis externa, often after prolonged antibiotic drops or in humid climates
• **Aspergillus niger** – black-grey spores on white hyphae (wet newspaper look); **Candida albicans** – white creamy debris
• Features: **intense itch**, pain, **ear blockage**, discharge
• Treatment: thorough **ear toilet** + **antifungal** drops/cream (e.g. clotrimazole)
• **Stop antibiotic drops** – they encourage fungal overgrowth
cards.m: Black spores = Aspergillus niger; itch more than pain = think fungus.

cards.q: What ear care advice should you give patients with ear infection?
cards.a:
• **Water precautions**: ear plug or cotton wool soaked in oil when bathing, avoid swimming, avoid washing inside the ear during ablution
• **Do not dig** the ear with cotton buds or metal objects
• Avoid **prolonged use of headphones/ear buds**, and keep them clean
• Use ear drops correctly: lie with the ear up for a few minutes, press the tragus to pump drops in, complete the course
cards.m: Dry, Don't dig, Disinfect earphones, Drops done properly.

cards.q: What is malignant (necrotising) otitis externa, and who gets it?
cards.a:
• Bacterial infection of the soft tissue of the external ear that **spreads to periosteum and bone of the skull base** (skull base osteomyelitis)
• 'Malignant' because of its aggressive course – **not a cancer**
• Typically **elderly diabetics** or the immunocompromised (HIV, chemotherapy)
• Organism: almost always **Pseudomonas aeruginosa**
• Spreads from the canal floor through the **fissures of Santorini** and the bony-cartilaginous junction (see also deck fnp)
cards.m: Old + Diabetic + Painful ear that will not settle = MOE until proven otherwise.

cards.q: What clinical features should make you suspect malignant otitis externa rather than simple otitis externa?
cards.a:
• **Excruciating, deep, nocturnal** otalgia out of proportion to the signs
• Persistent discharge despite more than a week of topical treatment
• **Granulation tissue on the floor of the canal** at the **bony-cartilaginous junction**
• **Cranial nerve palsy** – facial (VII) first (stylomastoid foramen), then IX, X, XI (jugular foramen) and XII
• Often little fever; ESR/CRP raised
cards.m: Granulation on the floor + night pain + facial palsy in a diabetic = skull base osteomyelitis.

cards.q: What are the Cohen & Friedman (1987) criteria for malignant otitis externa?
cards.a:
• **Major (all required)**: **pain**, **oedema**, **exudate**, **granulations**, **microabscess** (at operation), **positive Tc-99m bone scan** or **failure of local treatment ≥ 1 week**
• **Minor**: **Pseudomonas** on culture, positive bone radiograph, **diabetes**, **cranial nerve involvement**, debilitating condition, **old age**
• Note: slide lists 'ESR (high)' as a minor criterion – ESR is **not** part of the original criteria; ESR/CRP are used to **monitor** treatment
cards.m: Majors = what you see and scan (pain, swelling, pus, granulation, abscess, scan/failure); minors = who the patient is.

cards.q: What investigations are done in suspected malignant otitis externa?
cards.a:
• Bloods: **FBC, ESR, CRP**, blood glucose/HbA1c
• **Swab C&S** – Pseudomonas and its sensitivities
• **Biopsy of the granulation tissue** – to exclude **squamous cell carcinoma** of the canal
• **HRCT temporal bone** (bone erosion) ± MRI (soft-tissue and marrow spread, intracranial extent) especially if complications
• Nuclear scan (Tc-99m for diagnosis – see next card)
cards.m: Bloods, Bug, Biopsy, Bone imaging.

cards.q: Technetium-99m vs gallium-67 scan in malignant otitis externa – what is each used for?
cards.a:
• **Tc-99m bone scan** shows osteoblastic activity → very sensitive for **diagnosis**, but stays **positive for months** even after cure
• **Gallium-67** (or indium-labelled WBC) scan shows active inflammation → used to **monitor response** and decide **when to stop antibiotics**
• Note: slide says the bone scan is for diagnosis and to evaluate response – correct is **Tc-99m to diagnose, gallium to monitor**
cards.m: Technetium = Tells you it's there; Gallium = Gone yet?

cards.q: How is malignant otitis externa treated?
cards.a:
• **Admit** – pain control, close monitoring
• **Systemic anti-pseudomonal antibiotic**: **ciprofloxacin**, typically **IV ~2 weeks then oral** – total about **6-8 weeks** (guided by culture)
• **Strict blood sugar control**
• **Regular ear toilet** + topical antibiotic drops
• **Monitor** symptoms, ESR/CRP and **gallium scan**
• Surgery only for biopsy/debridement of sequestrum or abscess
cards.m: Admit, Antibiotic for weeks, Aural toilet, Assess sugar, Assess response.

cards.q: Define otitis media with effusion (glue ear).
cards.a:
• Accumulation of **non-purulent (serous or mucoid) fluid** in the middle ear cleft
• **Without signs or symptoms of acute inflammation** (no fever, no acute pain, TM not inflamed)
• Commonest cause of **hearing loss in children**
cards.m: Fluid without fire.

cards.q: Why are otitis media with effusion and acute otitis media commoner in children?
cards.a:
• Child's **Eustachian tube is shorter, wider and more horizontal** → nasopharyngeal secretions and organisms reach the middle ear easily, and drainage is poor
• Tube opening muscle (tensor veli palatini) is less efficient
• **Adenoids** are large and harbour bacteria/obstruct the tube
• Frequent URTIs and immature immunity
cards.m: Short, Wide, Flat tube = an open door to the middle ear.

cards.q: What are the risk factors for otitis media with effusion?
cards.a:
• **Eustachian tube dysfunction**
• **Allergy** / allergic rhinitis
• **Unresolved acute otitis media**
• **Nasal or nasopharyngeal obstruction** – allergic rhinitis, **adenoid hypertrophy**, nasopharyngeal mass
• **Craniofacial anomalies** – **cleft lip/palate**, **Down syndrome**
• Others: passive smoking, day-care attendance, bottle feeding
cards.m: Anything that blocks or weakens the tube: Tube, Allergy, Adenoid, Cleft, Down.

cards.q: An adult presents with unilateral otitis media with effusion. What must you exclude, and how?
cards.a:
• **Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC)** – tumour in the fossa of Rosenmüller blocks the Eustachian tube
• Very high-yield in Malaysia (high incidence, especially in Chinese and Bidayuh populations)
• Ask about epistaxis, nasal blockage, neck lump, cranial nerve symptoms
• **Nasoendoscopy of the postnasal space** ± biopsy; EBV serology; examine the neck
• Never just insert a grommet without looking at the nasopharynx
cards.m: Adult + one glue ear = look behind the nose (NPC).

cards.q: What are the clinical features of otitis media with effusion in children?
cards.a:
• **Reduced hearing** – often noticed by parents or teachers ('not listening', TV volume up)
• Ear blockage, mild otalgia
• **Speech and language delay**
• **Poor performance at school**, behavioural problems
• Often bilateral and painless – may be picked up on screening
cards.m: Quiet child, quiet ears: a hearing problem until proven otherwise.

cards.q: What does the tympanic membrane look like in otitis media with effusion?
cards.a:
• **Dull, yellowish/amber, opaque** TM
• **Diffuse (lost) cone of light**
• **Air-fluid level** or **air bubbles** behind the drum
• Usually **retracted** with reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy; occasionally bulging
• Often associated with **adenoid hypertrophy**
cards.m: Amber drum with a fluid line = glue.

cards.q: What do tuning fork tests, PTA and tympanometry show in otitis media with effusion?
cards.a:
• Tuning forks: **Rinne negative**, **Weber to the affected ear** → conductive loss
• PTA: **conductive hearing loss** (air-bone gap), typically 20-40 dB
• Tympanometry: **type B (flat)** with **normal ear canal volume**
• Normal ECV distinguishes effusion from perforation (high ECV) or wax (low ECV)
cards.m: Flat line, Normal volume = fluid behind an intact drum.

cards.q: What is the initial (non-surgical) management of otitis media with effusion?
cards.a:
• **Active observation for 3 months** – most effusions resolve spontaneously
• Repeat hearing test at the end of the period; advise on classroom seating and speaking clearly
• Patients with **allergic symptoms**: treat the allergy – **intranasal steroid**, antihistamine
• Antibiotics, decongestants and antihistamines do **not** clear the effusion itself
• Hearing aid is an alternative to surgery
cards.m: Watch and wait 3 months – glue usually dissolves.

cards.q: When is grommet insertion indicated in otitis media with effusion, and where is it placed?
cards.a:
• Indication: **persistent OME after 3 months** with **CHL > 25 dB** (bilateral, or with speech/educational impact)
• **Myringotomy and grommet (ventilation tube)** in the **anteroinferior quadrant** – away from the ossicles and chorda tympani and least likely to injure the stapes or round window
• Grommet **ventilates** the middle ear, bypassing the faulty Eustachian tube; extrudes in 6-12 months
• **+ Adenoidectomy** if adenoid hypertrophy (also lowers recurrence)
cards.m: 3 months, 25 dB, Anteroinferior: the grommet rule.

cards.q: What is otitis media, and how are acute and chronic otitis media separated by time?
cards.a:
• **Otitis media** = generic term for **all types of inflammation of the middle ear**
• **Acute**: ear symptoms present **< 3 weeks**
• **Chronic**: ear symptoms present **> 3 months**
• (Between these, some texts use 'subacute')
cards.m: Acute = under 3 weeks; Chronic = over 3 months.

cards.q: Who typically gets acute otitis media, and which organisms cause it?
cards.a:
• Peak in **children 6 months-2 years**, usually after a **viral URTI**
• Commonest bacteria: **Streptococcus pneumoniae**, **non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae**, **Moraxella catarrhalis** (also Group A Strep)
• Route: up the **Eustachian tube** from the nasopharynx
• Risk factors: day care, passive smoking, bottle feeding lying flat, adenoids, cleft palate
cards.m: The 'big three': Pneumococcus, Haemophilus, Moraxella – same bugs as sinusitis.

cards.q: What are the four stages of acute otitis media?
cards.a:
• 1. Stage of **tubal occlusion**
• 2. Stage of **pre-suppuration**
• 3. Stage of **suppuration**
• 4. Stage of **resolution**
• (If untreated or virulent, it may progress to complications instead of resolution)
cards.m: Tube blocks → Pink drum → Pus (bulge) → Pops (perforation).

cards.q: Compare the stage of tubal occlusion with the stage of pre-suppuration in AOM.
cards.a:
• **Tubal occlusion**: Eustachian tube blocked by **oedema of the nasopharynx** → air absorbed → **TM retracted**; reduced hearing and otalgia
• **Pre-suppuration**: prolonged occlusion → **invasion by pyogenic organisms** → inflammatory exudate in the middle ear → **congested, hyperaemic TM** (cartwheel vessels); otalgia, reduced hearing, tinnitus
cards.m: Stage 1 the drum is sucked In; stage 2 it turns Red.

cards.q: What happens in the stage of suppuration of AOM, and what are its features?
cards.a:
• **Pus forms in the middle ear** under pressure
• **Bulging TM** (red/yellow, loss of landmarks)
• **Otalgia at its worst** (increasing intensity), reduced hearing
• **Fever**, irritability, unwell child
• This is the stage at which **myringotomy** may be needed to relieve pain
cards.m: Bulge = worst pain, highest fever.

cards.q: What happens in the stage of resolution of AOM?
cards.a:
• **TM ruptures** → pus released → inflammatory process starts to resolve
• **Pain reduces** suddenly, followed by **ear discharge** (often blood-stained then mucopurulent)
• Exam: **TM perforation** (small, usually central) with an inflamed TM
• Most perforations heal spontaneously within weeks
cards.m: Pop = relief: the pain stops when the drum bursts.

cards.q: What are the symptoms and signs of acute otitis media, especially in children?
cards.a:
• Otalgia (young children **rub or pull the ear**), ear fullness, reduced hearing
• **Fever**, **irritability**, poor feeding, unwell child
• ± Ear discharge
• TM: **inflamed, bulging with pus behind an intact drum**, or **perforated with pus discharge**
cards.m: Fever + ear-tugging + bulging red drum = AOM.

cards.q: What is the medical treatment of acute otitis media?
cards.a:
• **Analgesia** (paracetamol/ibuprofen) – the mainstay
• **Oral amoxicillin** first line (5-7 days; longer if < 2 years or severe); amoxicillin-clavulanate if failure; or **watchful waiting** 48-72 h in selected older, well children
• **Topical antibiotic drops** (non-ototoxic **quinolone**) only if the TM is **perforated/discharging**
• Treat associated URTI symptomatically
• Note: slide lists antihistamine for URTI – **antihistamines and decongestants have no proven benefit in AOM**
cards.m: Pain relief + Amoxicillin; drops only if the drum has a hole.

cards.q: When is myringotomy indicated in AOM, and which features mean complicated disease needing urgent referral?
cards.a:
• **Myringotomy**: **severe pain with a bulging TM** (releases pus, relieves pain, gives a culture specimen); failed medical treatment
• Refer urgently if: **postauricular swelling/tenderness** (mastoiditis), **facial palsy**, vertigo, severe headache, neck stiffness, drowsiness (intracranial spread)
• Persistent discharge > 3 weeks or effusion > 3 months → review for COM/OME
cards.m: Bulging + agony = let it out; swelling behind the ear or a weak face = refer today.

cards.q: Define chronic otitis media.
cards.a:
• **Chronic inflammation of the middle ear and mastoid mucosa**
• In which the **tympanic membrane is not intact (perforation)**
• With **discharge (otorrhoea) for > 3 months** when active
• May be **active** (discharging) or **inactive** (dry perforation)
cards.m: COM = Chronic hole + On-and-off discharge for More than 3 months.

cards.q: What are the features of tubotympanic (safe) chronic otitis media?
cards.a:
• Discharge: **profuse, mucoid, odourless**
• Perforation: **central** (rim of TM all round)
• Granulation tissue: **uncommon**
• Cholesteatoma: **absent**
• Complications: **rare**
• Disease of the mucosa of the anteroinferior middle ear cleft (tubotympanum)
cards.m: Safe = Central, Copious, no smell.

cards.q: What are the features of atticoantral (unsafe) chronic otitis media?
cards.a:
• Discharge: **scanty, purulent, foul-smelling** (anaerobes + keratin)
• Perforation: **marginal** or **attic (pars flaccida)**
• Granulation tissue and aural polyps: **common**
• Cholesteatoma: **frequent**
• Complications: **common** – because bone is eroded
• 'Unsafe' = squamous disease of the attic, antrum and mastoid
cards.m: Unsafe = Scanty, Smelly, at the Side (marginal) or attic.

cards.q: How are the complications of chronic otitis media classified?
cards.a:
• **Extracranial – intratemporal**: acute mastoiditis/mastoid abscess, labyrinthitis, petrositis, facial nerve palsy
• **Extracranial – extratemporal**: postauricular, **Bezold**, **Citelli**, **Luc**, zygomatic and retromastoid abscesses
• **Intracranial**: meningitis, extradural abscess, subdural abscess, otogenic brain abscess, **lateral sinus thrombophlebitis**, otitic hydrocephalus
cards.m: Think concentric rings: inside the temporal bone → outside it in the neck/face → inside the skull.

cards.q: What are the signs of acute mastoiditis with mastoid abscess?
cards.a:
• **Pinna pushed forwards and downwards** (outwards)
• **Swelling over the mastoid** – tender, fluctuant, erythematous; postauricular sulcus obliterated
• **Sagging of the posterosuperior meatal wall** on otoscopy (periosteum of the antrum pushed down)
• Plus fever, worsening otalgia and discharge
cards.m: Sag of the posterosuperior wall = pus in the antrum next door.

cards.q: What is Gradenigo's syndrome?
cards.a:
• Complication of **petrositis** (infection of the petrous apex air cells)
• Triad: **persistent otorrhoea**, **pain in the CN V distribution** (retro-orbital/deep facial pain – Gasserian ganglion), **lateral rectus palsy (CN VI)** → diplopia
• CN VI is hit as it runs through **Dorello's canal** over the petrous apex
cards.m: Gradenigo: Gunk (otorrhoea), Grimace (V pain), Gaze palsy (VI).

cards.q: Facial nerve palsy in chronic otitis media: why does it happen and how is it managed?
cards.a:
• Cholesteatoma or granulation erodes the bony **Fallopian canal** (tympanic segment) and inflames the nerve
• Facial palsy in COM is an **indication for urgent surgery** (mastoid exploration and decompression) – not 'Bell's palsy'
• Medical: **systemic steroid**, IV antibiotic, **facial physiotherapy**, **eye care – eye padding and artificial tears**
• See deck fnp for nerve tests and grading
cards.m: A weak face with a smelly ear = cholesteatoma until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Where do Bezold, Citelli, Luc and zygomatic abscesses point?
cards.a:
• **Bezold**: pus breaks through the **mastoid tip** medially → **deep to sternocleidomastoid** (neck swelling)
• **Citelli**: through the medial mastoid → **digastric triangle**
• **Luc**: from the antrum via the **roof of the EAC** → **deep to temporalis**, no postauricular swelling
• **Zygomatic**: via zygomatic air cells → swelling **in front of/above the ear**
• **Postauricular** abscess is the commonest
cards.m: Bezold = Below (neck, under SCM); Luc = Lateral roof of canal under temporalis.

cards.q: Which features in a patient with chronic otitis media suggest intracranial spread?
cards.a:
• **Persistent headache**, high or swinging fever, vomiting
• **Neck stiffness**, photophobia (meningitis)
• **Drowsiness**, confusion, seizures, focal signs (brain abscess – temporal lobe or cerebellum)
• Papilloedema, sixth nerve palsy (raised ICP, otitic hydrocephalus)
• Action: admit, IV antibiotics, **urgent CT/MRI brain** with HRCT temporal bone, neurosurgical input
cards.m: Smelly ear + headache = CT the head, not paracetamol.

cards.q: What are the features of lateral (sigmoid) sinus thrombophlebitis as a complication of otitis media?
cards.a:
• Infected thrombus in the sigmoid/lateral sinus adjacent to the mastoid
• **'Picket-fence' fever** with rigors (septic emboli)
• **Griesinger sign**: oedema and tenderness over the mastoid emissary vein (posterior mastoid)
• Tobey-Ayer test (CSF pressure), papilloedema, possible otitic hydrocephalus
• Diagnosis: **CT/MR venography** ('empty delta' sign); Rx: IV antibiotics + mastoidectomy ± anticoagulation
cards.m: Picket-fence fever = a fence of spikes from an infected venous sinus.

cards.q: How is chronic otitis media categorised for management, and how is inactive (dry) COM managed?
cards.a:
• Categories: **inactive**, **active without complication**, **active with complication**
• **Inactive (dry perforation)**:
• **Audiometry** (baseline hearing)
• **Keep the ear dry** (water precautions)
• After about **6 months dry**, offer **myringoplasty** (graft – usually temporalis fascia – to close the perforation)
cards.m: Dry for 6 months → patch the hole.

cards.q: How is active chronic otitis media without complication managed?
cards.a:
• **Ear toilet/mopping** (microsuction) – the key step
• **Topical** antibiotic drops – **better than oral** (very high local concentration): **ofloxacin ear drops**
• **Keep the ear dry**
• **Pus swab C&S only for unresolved cases**
• Observe for complications and follow up
cards.m: Clean, Drop, Dry – then Follow.

cards.q: In active chronic otitis media, when are systemic antibiotics added, and why prefer quinolone drops?
cards.a:
• Systemic antibiotics: **paediatric** patients, **granulation tissue**, or **not resolving with topical antibiotic alone**
• **Quinolone drops (ofloxacin, ciprofloxacin)** are **not ototoxic** and cover Pseudomonas
• **Aminoglycoside drops** (gentamicin, neomycin) risk **cochlear/vestibular toxicity** through a perforation – avoid when the TM is not intact if possible
cards.m: Hole in the drum? Pick a Quinolone, not an aminoglycoside.

cards.q: How is active chronic otitis media with complication managed?
cards.a:
• Investigations: **pus swab**, **HRCT temporal bone ± brain** imaging, **audiometry**
• Medical: **admit**, **systemic (IV) antibiotic**, topical drops, ear toilet
• Facial palsy: systemic steroid, facial physiotherapy, eye padding, artificial tears
• Surgical: **cortical mastoidectomy** (drain mastoid); canal wall down/modified radical if cholesteatoma
• Drain abscesses; neurosurgery for intracranial collections
cards.m: Complication = Admit, IV, Image, Operate.

cards.q: What is a cholesteatoma, and why is it destructive?
cards.a:
• **'Skin in the wrong place'**
• Epidermal cyst of the middle ear and/or temporal bone with a **keratinising squamous epithelial lining**, containing **keratin and desquamated epithelium**
• Natural history: **progressive growth with bone erosion** by **pressure** and **osteoclast activation** (enzymes from the inflamed matrix)
• Erodes ossicles, scutum, lateral SCC, facial canal, tegmen, sigmoid plate → complications
cards.m: A skin bag that keeps filling with dead skin and eats bone.

cards.q: How are cholesteatomas classified?
cards.a:
• **Congenital** – arises behind an **intact TM** from embryonic epithelial rests
• **Acquired**:
• a) **Primary acquired** – from a **retraction pocket**, no preceding infection or perforation
• b) **Secondary acquired** – from a **perforation** after previous infection
cards.m: Congenital = behind intact drum; Primary = Pocket; Secondary = perforation.

cards.q: What are the Levenson criteria for congenital cholesteatoma?
cards.a:
• **White mass medial to a normal TM**
• **Normal pars tensa and pars flaccida**
• **No history of otorrhoea or perforation**
• **No prior otological procedure**
• Classically a pearly white mass in the **anterosuperior quadrant** in a child
cards.m: White pearl behind a perfect drum, in an ear that has never been sick or operated on.

cards.q: What is primary acquired cholesteatoma, and which theories explain it?
cards.a:
• Arises from a **retraction pocket** (usually **pars flaccida/attic**) due to Eustachian tube dysfunction and negative pressure
• **Infection has not given rise** to it (no previous perforation)
• Theories: **invagination/retraction pocket (Wittmaack)** and **basal cell hyperplasia (Ruedi)** – keratinocytes of the pars flaccida proliferate into the attic
• Note: slide groups Ruedi under secondary acquired; most texts (Dhingra) place **basal cell hyperplasia under PRIMARY acquired**
cards.m: Primary = Pocket: Wittmaack sucks it in, Ruedi grows it in.

cards.q: What is secondary acquired cholesteatoma, and which theories explain it?
cards.a:
• Arises through a **perforation** of the TM (usually **marginal** posterosuperior)
• **Previous ear infection** is present
• Theories: **epithelial invasion/migration (Habermann)** – canal/TM skin grows in through the perforation edge
• **Squamous metaplasia** of middle ear mucosa after chronic infection (**Sadé**)
• (Basal cell hyperplasia – Ruedi – is usually grouped with primary acquired)
cards.m: Secondary = skin migrates through a hole (Habermann) or mucosa Switches to skin (Sadé).

cards.q: What is the Sadé classification of pars tensa retraction?
cards.a:
• **Grade 1** – slight retraction of the TM
• **Grade 2** – severe retraction, TM **touching the incus or stapes**
• **Grade 3** – **atelectasis**: TM touching the **promontory** (but not stuck)
• **Grade 4** – **adhesive otitis**: TM **adherent to the promontory**
• Deep, non-self-cleaning pockets can collect keratin → cholesteatoma
cards.m: Sadé for Tensa: slight → ossicles → promontory touch → promontory stuck.

cards.q: What is the Tos classification of pars flaccida (attic) retraction?
cards.a:
• **Grade 1** – retracted pars flaccida **not in contact** with the neck of malleus
• **Grade 2** – **in contact with the neck of malleus**
• **Grade 3** – as grade 2 plus **limited erosion of the outer attic wall (scutum)**
• **Grade 4** – as grade 3 plus **severe erosion** of the outer attic wall/scutum
• Erosion of the scutum marks the shift towards cholesteatoma
cards.m: Tos for the Top (attic): 1 free, 2 touching malleus, 3 nibbling the scutum, 4 eating it.

cards.q: What are the symptoms and otoscopic signs of cholesteatoma?
cards.a:
• Symptoms: **scanty, foul-smelling otorrhoea**, bleeding, **hearing loss**, otalgia, tinnitus, **vertigo** (fistula)
• Signs: **attic retraction/perforation** or **marginal perforation**
• **Pearly white cholesteatoma flakes** with a fishy odour
• **Granulation tissue**, **attic polyp**
• Scanty, purulent, foul discharge
cards.m: Smelly, scanty, and white flakes in the attic.

cards.q: Why must the attic always be examined even when a central perforation is seen?
cards.a:
• An **attic cholesteatoma sac** can coexist with a pars tensa (central) perforation
• Seeing a 'safe' central perforation can falsely reassure – the attic disease is easily missed behind a crust or polyp
• Clear crusts at the **pars flaccida** with microsuction under the microscope
• Large attic cholesteatomas may expose the **head of malleus** or extend into the mesotympanum
cards.m: Never stop at the first hole – always look upstairs (attic).

cards.q: Which investigations are done for cholesteatoma, and what are the other indications for HRCT temporal bone?
cards.a:
• **HRCT temporal bone** – extent of disease and nearby anatomy (surgical roadmap)
• **Swab C&S**; **HPE of granulation tissue** to exclude malignancy; audiometry
• Other HRCT indications: **suspected complications**, **revision surgery**, **TM not visualised**/indeterminate exam, **children** (exclude petrous apex lesion), **only or better-hearing ear**
cards.m: Scan when it's Complicated, Revised, Can't be seen, a Child, or the Crucial (only) ear.

cards.q: What are the HRCT hallmarks of cholesteatoma, and what is the earliest sign?
cards.a:
• **Soft-tissue mass** with homogeneous opacity and **sharp, defined borders**, especially in the **attic and non-dependent** areas (fluid lies dependent)
• **Bone erosion** of the **scutum**, incus and malleus, or mastoid air cells
• **Blunting of the scutum** is often the **earliest sign**
• Also look at lateral SCC (fistula), tegmen, facial canal, sigmoid plate
cards.m: Blunt scutum = the first bite of cholesteatoma.

cards.q: What is the role of medical versus surgical treatment in cholesteatoma?
cards.a:
• Medical (holding measures only): **regular microsuction clearance** and follow-up, **topical ear drops**, **strict dry-ear precautions** – for the unfit, or to quieten the ear before surgery
• **Surgery is the mainstay: mastoidectomy**
• Presence of cholesteatoma **mandates surgery** – there is **no medical alternative** that removes the disease
• Aims: safe dry ear first, hearing second
cards.m: Drops dry it, only a drill removes it.

cards.q: Canal wall-up versus canal wall-down mastoidectomy – what is the difference and which operations are in each group?
cards.a:
• **Canal wall-up**: **preserves the posterior wall of the EAC** – atticotomy, attico-antrostomy, **cortical (Schwartze) mastoidectomy**, **combined approach tympanoplasty**
• Normal-looking canal, no cavity care, but higher **residual/recurrent** disease → second-look surgery
• **Canal wall-down**: posterior canal wall removed – **radical** and **modified radical mastoidectomy**
• Best exposure and lower recurrence, but leaves an open **mastoid cavity** needing lifelong care
cards.m: Wall Up = looks normal, may hide disease; Wall Down = open cavity, nowhere to hide.

cards.q: Radical versus modified radical mastoidectomy – what is the key difference?
cards.a:
• **Radical**: eradicates disease from middle ear and mastoid **without reconstructing hearing** – posterior meatal wall removed; middle ear, attic, antrum and mastoid made **one cavity**; TM remnants, ossicles (**except stapes footplate**) and mucosa removed; **Eustachian tube obliterated** with muscle/cartilage
• **Modified radical**: same cavity but **hearing mechanism preserved** as much as possible – TM remnants and ossicles (especially **handle of malleus and stapes**)
• Further modification: TM grafting and ossicular reconstruction = **mastoidectomy with tympanoplasty**
cards.m: Radical = clear everything, sacrifice hearing; Modified = clear disease, keep what hears.

cards.q: What is vertigo, and what must you distinguish it from in a 'dizzy' patient?
cards.a:
• Vertigo is a **symptom, not a disease**
• **True vertigo** = an **illusion of movement**, usually spinning (self or surroundings)
• Distinguish from **light-headedness**, **presyncope** (about to faint – cardiovascular, postural hypotension) and **imbalance/unsteadiness while walking**
• Then decide: **peripheral** (labyrinth/vestibular nerve) or **central** (brainstem/cerebellum) cause
cards.m: Spinning = vestibular; swooning = circulation; staggering = gait/neurology.

cards.q: What do the semicircular canals, utricle and saccule each detect?
cards.a:
• **Semicircular canals** (3, at right angles; crista ampullaris) → **angular (rotational) acceleration**
• **Otolith organs** (maculae with otoconia) → **linear acceleration** and gravity:
• **Utricle** → **horizontal** linear movement (**forward-backward**)
• **Saccule** → **vertical** linear movement (**up-down**, e.g. a lift)
cards.m: Canals = Turning; Utricle = forward in a car; Saccule = up in a lift.

cards.q: What are the vestibulo-ocular and vestibulospinal reflexes?
cards.a:
• **VOR (vestibulo-ocular reflex)**: keeps the **eyes stable on a target during head movement** – eyes move equal and opposite to the head
• **VSR (vestibulospinal reflex)**: maintains **balance and posture** via antigravity muscles
• An acute unilateral vestibular loss upsets the VOR → **nystagmus** and oscillopsia; upsets the VSR → falling to the side of the lesion
cards.m: VOR steadies the camera (eyes); VSR steadies the tripod (body).

cards.q: List the main peripheral and central causes of vertigo.
cards.a:
• **Peripheral** (vestibular end-organ and nerve): **BPPV**, **Ménière's disease**, **labyrinthitis**, vestibular neuritis/vestibulopathy
• **Central** (brain/brainstem/cerebellum): **stroke** (posterior circulation), **tumour (acoustic neuroma** – vestibular schwannoma at the CP angle), **multiple sclerosis**, **vestibular migraine**
cards.m: Peripheral = BMLV; Central = Stroke, Schwannoma, Sclerosis, migraine.

cards.q: How does nystagmus help distinguish peripheral from central vertigo?
cards.a:
• **Peripheral**: **unidirectional** in all gaze positions, **horizontal-torsional (rotatory)**, **suppressed by visual fixation**, **fatigable**, appears after a **latency (lag)** on positional testing
• **Central**: **changes direction** with gaze position, may be **pure vertical** (down/upbeat) or pure torsional, **not suppressed by fixation**, non-fatigable, no latency
cards.m: Peripheral nystagmus is polite: one direction, tires out, hides when you stare. Central nystagmus is rude.

cards.q: Apart from nystagmus, which features separate peripheral from central vertigo?
cards.a:
• **Imbalance**: peripheral mild-moderate and **episodic**; central **severe, mostly constant** (may be unable to stand)
• **Neurological symptoms**: peripheral **rare**; central **frequent** (diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia, weakness)
• **Hearing loss**: peripheral **frequent**; central **rare**
• **Nausea/vomiting**: peripheral **severe**; central variable
• **Recovery by central compensation**: peripheral **rapid**; central **slow**
cards.m: Peripheral = sick and deaf but walks; Central = can't walk, has neuro signs.

cards.q: What is BPPV and what causes it?
cards.a:
• **Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo** – the **most common** cause of peripheral vertigo
• **Otoconia dislodged from the utricle** float into a semicircular canal (canalolithiasis) and make the cupula respond to gravity
• **Posterior semicircular canal in ~80%** (most dependent canal)
• Brief vertigo lasting **seconds (usually < 1 min)**, triggered by **head position** – rolling in bed, looking up, bending
• No hearing loss, no tinnitus
cards.m: Loose stones from the utricle roll down the posterior canal when you roll over in bed.

cards.q: How is the Dix-Hallpike test performed and what is a positive result for posterior canal BPPV?
cards.a:
• Patient sits; head turned **45°** to the test side; lie back quickly with the head **hanging ~20-30° below horizontal**
• Positive: after a **latency of a few seconds** → vertigo with **torsional, upbeating, geotropic nystagmus** (towards the lower ear)
• Lasts **< 1 minute**; **reverses** on sitting up; **fatigues on repetition**
• The **dependent (lower) ear** is the affected one
cards.m: Latent, Limited, Lessens (fatigues), Lower ear affected.

cards.q: What is the Epley manoeuvre and what advice follows it?
cards.a:
• **Canalith repositioning manoeuvre** for posterior canal BPPV
• Starts from the positive Dix-Hallpike position, then a series of head turns (90° to the other side, roll onto the side with the nose down, then sit up), holding each ~30-60 s
• Moves otoconia out of the posterior canal back into the **utricle**
• Success ~80% after 1-2 manoeuvres; may repeat; Brandt-Daroff exercises at home
• Vestibular sedatives are not needed and delay compensation
cards.m: Hallpike finds the stones; Epley puts them back.

cards.q: What is Ménière's disease and how does it present?
cards.a:
• **Idiopathic endolymphatic hydrops** (excess endolymph distending the membranous labyrinth)
• Triad: **episodic vertigo**, **fluctuating hearing loss with aural fullness**, **tinnitus**
• Hearing loss is **sensorineural**, typically **low-frequency** early, worsening progressively
• Associated **nausea and vomiting**
• Attacks last **20 minutes to 12 hours** (slide: minutes to hours) – much longer than BPPV seconds
cards.m: Ménière's = a waterlogged inner ear: Vertigo + Fullness + Tinnitus + Low-tone loss.

cards.q: What is the medical management of Ménière's disease?
cards.a:
• **Acute attack**: vestibular sedatives/antiemetics – **prochlorperazine**, **promethazine** – short term only (they delay compensation)
• **Prophylaxis**: **betahistine** (Betaserc)
• **Lifestyle**: **low-salt diet**, stop smoking and alcohol, limit caffeine
• **Vestibular rehabilitation**
• **Intratympanic steroid** (hearing-sparing) or **intratympanic gentamicin** (chemical labyrinthectomy – risks hearing) if attacks persist
cards.m: Acute: sedate; Long-term: Betahistine + low Salt; Resistant: drip into the drum.

cards.q: What surgical options exist for Ménière's disease, and when are they used?
cards.a:
• Only **if medical treatment fails** to control vertigo
• **Endolymphatic sac decompression** – conservative, hearing preserved
• **Vestibular neurectomy** – cuts the vestibular nerve, preserves hearing, controls vertigo
• **Labyrinthectomy** – destructive, only when hearing in that ear is already **non-serviceable**
• Choice depends on **hearing level** and the other ear
cards.m: Save hearing → sac or nerve cut; hearing already gone → destroy the labyrinth.

cards.q: How is labyrinthitis classified, and how do serous and suppurative labyrinthitis differ?
cards.a:
• **Infective**: suppurative (bacterial), serous (viral), circumscribed (focal), syphilitic, fungal
• **Non-infective (sterile)**: autoimmune, labyrinthitis ossificans, toxic/drug-induced
• **Serous (viral)**: inflammation without pus → vertigo with partial, often **recoverable** hearing loss
• **Suppurative (bacterial)**: pus in the labyrinth (from otitis media or meningitis) → severe vertigo and **total, permanent hearing loss** (dead ear)
cards.m: Serous = may Spare hearing; Suppurative = Sacrifices it.

cards.q: What is circumscribed labyrinthitis and how is it detected?
cards.a:
• **Focal inflammation of the bony labyrinth** – usually from **cholesteatoma eroding the lateral semicircular canal** (labyrinthine fistula)
• Brief vertigo on pressure changes: pressing the tragus, nose blowing, cleaning the ear
• **Positive fistula test**: pressure on the tragus/pneumatic speculum → vertigo and nystagmus
• Hearing usually preserved at first; HRCT confirms; needs **surgery** (remove matrix over the fistula carefully)
cards.m: Press the tragus, the eyes jump = a hole in the lateral canal.

cards.q: What is pure tone audiometry and what is it used for?
cards.a:
• **Subjective** test of a person's ability to hear pure tones of various frequencies, using an **audiometer** in a soundproof booth
• Determines:
• **Hearing threshold level** (quietest tone heard 50% of the time)
• **Type** of hearing loss
• **Severity** of hearing loss
• Needs a cooperative patient (usually from ~4-5 years)
cards.m: PTA answers 3 questions: How quiet? What type? How bad?

cards.q: Air conduction versus bone conduction on PTA – what does each tell you?
cards.a:
• **Air conduction (headphones)**: tests the whole pathway (outer + middle + inner ear) → **threshold level** and **severity** of hearing loss
• **Bone conduction (vibrator on mastoid)**: bypasses outer and middle ear → reflects **cochlear function** → determines the **type** of loss
• Types: **conductive**, **sensorineural**, **mixed**
cards.m: Air = How bad; Bone = What type (the cochlea's own reserve).

cards.q: What is plotted on a pure tone audiogram, and what are the standard symbols?
cards.a:
• A graph of **pure-tone thresholds**: **frequency (pitch)** on the x-axis, **125-8000 Hz**; **intensity (loudness)** on the y-axis, **-10 to 120 dB HL** (worse hearing plotted lower)
• Symbols: right AC **O** (red), left AC **X** (blue); right BC **<**, left BC **>**
• Masking used to stop the better ear hearing the test tone (bracket symbols for masked BC)
• Normal hearing: thresholds within **0-20 dB HL**
cards.m: Red Round Right; blue X for the Left.

cards.q: How is the severity of hearing loss graded (British Society of Audiology)?
cards.a:
• **Mild**: **20-40 dB HL**
• **Moderate**: **41-70 dB HL**
• **Severe**: **71-95 dB HL**
• **Profound**: **> 95 dB HL**
• (Grade on the average of thresholds at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 kHz)
cards.m: 20-40-70-95: each step is roughly a doubling of difficulty.

cards.q: What does conductive hearing loss look like on PTA, and what are its common causes?
cards.a:
• **BC within normal range**; **AC abnormal** → an **air-bone gap** (more than about **10 dB**)
• Cochlea is normal – sound is blocked in the outer or middle ear
• Causes: **wax**, **foreign body**, **middle ear effusion**, **haemotympanum**, **chronic otitis media**, otosclerosis
• Note: slides give the gap as '≥ 10 dB' (p85) and '> 10 dB' (p91) – read it as a gap of more than about 10 dB with normal BC
cards.m: Bone normal, Air down = a blockage before the cochlea.

cards.q: What does sensorineural hearing loss look like on PTA, and what are its causes and classic patterns?
cards.a:
• **BC and AC both abnormal**, **no air-bone gap** (BC = AC)
• Lesion in the **cochlea or VIII nerve**; outer/middle ear clear
• Causes: congenital, **presbycusis**, **sudden SNHL**, **noise-induced**, **drug-induced** (aminoglycosides, cisplatin), autoimmune
• Patterns: **noise-induced = notch at 4 kHz**; **presbycusis = bilateral high-frequency sloping loss**; Ménière's = low-frequency loss
• **Unilateral/asymmetric SNHL** → MRI internal acoustic meatus (acoustic neuroma)
cards.m: Noise Notches at 4 k; age Slopes down at the high end.

cards.q: What is mixed hearing loss, and which condition typically causes it?
cards.a:
• **Both conductive and sensorineural** components
• **AC and BC both abnormal**, **with an air-bone gap** (AC worse than BC)
• Typical cause: **chronic otitis media ± cholesteatoma** (conductive from perforation/ossicular erosion + sensorineural from toxins entering through the round window or labyrinthine fistula)
• Also advanced otosclerosis
cards.m: Mixed = everything is down, but Air is down further.

cards.q: How do the 512 Hz tuning fork tests separate conductive from sensorineural hearing loss, and which hearing loss is an emergency?
cards.a:
• **Rinne negative** (BC > AC) + **Weber lateralises to the affected ear** → **conductive** loss in that ear
• **Rinne positive** (AC > BC) + **Weber lateralises to the better ear** → **sensorineural** loss in the other ear
• Normal: Rinne positive, Weber central
• **Sudden SNHL** (≥ 30 dB over 3 frequencies within 72 h) → **urgent ENT referral** for PTA and **steroids** (oral or intratympanic) as early as possible
cards.m: Weber goes to the Worse ear in conductive loss, and Away from it in sensorineural loss.

cards.q: What does tympanometry measure, and how is a tympanogram read?
cards.a:
• Measures how the **acoustic immittance (compliance)** of the middle ear changes as **air pressure in the ear canal is varied**
• Objective – no response needed from the patient
• Tympanogram: **compliance (ml)** on the y-axis vs **canal pressure (daPa)** on the x-axis (about -300 to +200)
• Read both the **shape** (type) and the numbers: **peak pressure**, **static compliance (SC)**, **ear canal volume (ECV)**
cards.m: The drum moves best when pressure on both sides is equal – the peak tells you the middle ear pressure.

cards.q: What is a type A tympanogram and what are the normal values?
cards.a:
• **Normal** middle ear pressure and TM compliance – normal middle ear function
• **Peak pressure: +50 to -100 daPa**
• **Static compliance: 0.3-1.7 ml**
• **Ear canal volume: 0.3-2.0 cm³** (smaller in children)
• Note: a type A does **not** exclude sensorineural loss
cards.m: A = All right.

cards.q: Type As versus type Ad tympanogram – what is the difference and the typical causes?
cards.a:
• Both have a **normal peak pressure (~0 daPa)** and normal ECV
• **As (shallow/stiff)**: **unusually low compliance** → stiff middle ear system – **otosclerosis** (stapes fixation), **tympanosclerosis**
• **Ad (deep)**: **markedly increased compliance** → flaccid/hypermobile system – **ossicular discontinuity**, thin scarred (atrophic) TM
cards.m: As = Stiff/Shallow (Stapes fixed); Ad = Deep/Disrupted ossicles.

cards.q: A flat (type B) tympanogram – how do you use the ear canal volume to interpret it?
cards.a:
• Type B = **no peak**: the TM does not move at any pressure
• **Normal ECV** → **middle ear effusion** (OME)
• **Low ECV** → **impacted wax** or probe against the canal wall
• **High ECV** → **TM perforation** or a **patent grommet** (probe measures canal + middle ear + mastoid)
• Note: slide headlines type B as 'normal ECV' – the ECV varies with the cause and is the key to interpretation
cards.m: Flat line? Check the Volume: Normal = fluid, Low = wax, High = hole.

cards.q: What is a type C tympanogram and what does it indicate?
cards.a:
• **Peak at abnormally negative pressure** (below about -100 daPa) with **normal SC and ECV**
• The drum moves best when canal pressure is negative → middle ear pressure is **below atmospheric**
• Indicates **Eustachian tube dysfunction**, with or without early middle ear fluid
• Seen with URTI, allergic rhinitis, adenoids, early or resolving OME; may progress to type B
cards.m: C = Collapsing (negative) pressure from a blocked tube.

cards.q: Combine PTA and tympanometry: what diagnosis fits each pattern of conductive hearing loss?
cards.a:
• CHL + **type B, normal ECV** → **otitis media with effusion**
• CHL + **type B, high ECV** → **TM perforation** (e.g. COM)
• CHL + **type As**, intact normal TM → **otosclerosis**
• CHL + **type Ad**, intact TM (e.g. after head injury) → **ossicular discontinuity**
• Mild CHL + **type C** → **Eustachian tube dysfunction**
cards.m: PTA says how much and what type; the tympanogram says where in the middle ear.

mcq.stem:
A 19-year-old university rugby player attends the ENT clinic the morning after a match. The left pinna is painful, with a smooth, tense, fluctuant purple swelling filling the scaphoid fossa and concha and obscuring the normal contours. There is no fever and the skin is intact.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral flucloxacillin, cold compress and review in one week
Observation, as the swelling will resorb within a fortnight
Needle aspiration, then a firm compression bolster dressing
Warm compress, an oral NSAID and strapping of the ear
Elective excision of the deformed cartilage once settled
mcq.e: This is an **auricular haematoma**: blood collects between perichondrium and cartilage and strips the cartilage of its blood supply. It must be evacuated early (aspirate; incise and drain with a button stitch if it recurs) and the space closed with **compression**, with oral antibiotic cover (slide p6). Left alone, the cartilage necroses and fibroses into a **cauliflower ear**.
w: Wrong - antibiotics and cold compress do not evacuate the blood; the cartilage will still lose its supply.
Wrong - a tense subperichondrial haematoma does not resorb safely; it organises into a cauliflower ear.
Correct - evacuate early and compress the space so the perichondrium re-adheres to the cartilage.
Wrong - heat and strapping without drainage leave the collection in place.
Wrong - this treats the end result (cauliflower ear) instead of preventing it.

mcq.stem:
A 22-year-old woman presents to the ED 5 days after a high helical (upper cartilage) piercing at a shopping-mall kiosk. The upper pinna is red, hot, swollen and exquisitely tender, but the lobule looks normal. There is no fluctuation. Temperature 37.9 °C.
Which organism should the empirical antibiotic primarily cover?
o: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Haemophilus influenzae
Aspergillus niger
Moraxella catarrhalis
mcq.e: Sparing of the **lobule** (which contains no cartilage) localises the infection to the perichondrium: **perichondritis**. After cartilage piercing the classic pathogen is **Pseudomonas aeruginosa**, so give a systemic anti-pseudomonal antibiotic such as oral **ciprofloxacin** (slide p5: systemic antibiotic) and drain any abscess. Undertreated, it destroys cartilage and deforms the ear.
w: Correct - Pseudomonas is the typical organism in perichondritis after high cartilage piercing; cover it with ciprofloxacin.
Wrong - a middle ear and chest pathogen, not the typical cause of pinna perichondritis.
Wrong - a cause of AOM and sinusitis, not perichondritis after piercing.
Wrong - a fungus of the canal (otomycosis), not of cartilage.
Wrong - an AOM organism; it does not cause perichondritis.

mcq.stem:
An 8-year-old boy is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan with a 3-day painful swelling just in front of the right ear, at the anterior margin of the ascending helix. It is red and fluctuant. His mother says a tiny pit has been there since birth and has discharged cheesy material twice before.
What is the best next step?
o: Reassure, as the pit is congenital and needs no treatment
Complete excision of the sinus tract during this admission
Topical antibiotic ointment into the pit and early review
Incision and drainage with a course of systemic antibiotics
Injection of a sclerosant into the tract under anaesthesia
mcq.e: An asymptomatic **preauricular sinus** needs no treatment, but an acute **preauricular abscess** is treated with **I&D and antibiotics** first (slide p8). Excision of the whole tract (followed down to the temporalis fascia) is for **recurrent** infection and is done once inflammation has settled, because dissecting through inflamed tissue leaves remnants that cause recurrence. This boy will need elective excision later.
w: Wrong - reassurance fits an uninfected pit, not a fluctuant abscess.
Wrong - excising through acute inflammation risks incomplete removal and recurrence; excise once quiet.
Wrong - topical treatment does not drain pus from a fluctuant abscess.
Correct - drain the abscess and give antibiotics now; plan tract excision when settled.
Wrong - sclerotherapy is not a treatment for a preauricular sinus.

mcq.stem:
A 60-year-old retired teacher at the ENT clinic has had a blocked left ear for 2 weeks. He had a left mastoid operation 10 years ago. Otoscopy shows hard impacted wax filling the canal; the drum cannot be seen. He has already used olive oil drops for a week.
Which is the most appropriate method of wax removal?
o: Ear syringing with water warmed to body temperature
Microsuction under the operating microscope
Hydrogen peroxide drops followed by irrigation
Self-cleaning with cotton buds after a hot shower
Electronic pulsed irrigator set at low pressure
mcq.e: Irrigation (syringing) is **contraindicated** after previous ear surgery, with a known or suspected **perforation**, a **grommet**, an **only-hearing ear** or acute otitis externa, because water can enter the middle ear or mastoid cavity and cause infection, vertigo or trauma. After softening drops (olive oil, sodium bicarbonate), **microsuction** under direct vision is the safe option. Cotton buds push wax deeper and are never advised (slide p64).
w: Wrong - syringing is contraindicated after mastoid surgery or when the drum cannot be confirmed intact.
Correct - microsuction under vision avoids forcing water into a possible cavity or perforation.
Wrong - this still ends in irrigation, which is contraindicated here.
Wrong - cotton buds impact wax and injure the canal skin.
Wrong - an irrigator at any pressure is still irrigation, contraindicated after ear surgery.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old man in Kota Bharu has 3 days of severe right earache, worse when he chews. Pulling the pinna is very painful. Otoscopy with a small speculum shows a single red, dome-shaped swelling on the posterior wall of the outer part of the canal; the deeper canal and drum are normal. Hearing is normal.
Which organism is most likely responsible?
o: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Aspergillus niger
Candida albicans
Proteus mirabilis
Staphylococcus aureus
mcq.e: A localised tender swelling in the outer canal is a **furuncle**, an infected hair follicle. It can arise only in the **outer cartilaginous third**, where hair and ceruminous glands are found, and the organism is **Staphylococcus aureus** (slide p11). Treat with analgesia and oral/topical anti-staphylococcal antibiotic, with I&D if fluctuant. Pseudomonas is the main cause of **diffuse** otitis externa involving the whole canal.
w: Wrong - Pseudomonas causes diffuse otitis externa, not a single localised follicular abscess.
Wrong - Aspergillus causes otomycosis (itch, blockage, black spores), not a furuncle.
Wrong - Candida causes white fungal debris, not a tender follicular abscess.
Wrong - a Gram-negative organism of diffuse otitis externa, not of furuncles.
Correct - a furuncle is a Staph aureus infection of a hair follicle in the outer canal.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old swimming instructor has 4 days of left ear pain, itch and discharge. Pressing the tragus is very painful. The whole canal is red and so swollen with debris that only a slit remains; the drum cannot be seen. She is afebrile, not diabetic, with no neck nodes or cellulitis.
After aural toilet, what is the best next step?
o: Start oral amoxicillin and review in two weeks
Syringe the canal to clear debris and see the drum
Insert an ear wick and soak it with quinolone drops
Prescribe gentamicin drops to instil into the canal
Book urgent CT of the temporal bone for bone disease
mcq.e: Diffuse **otitis externa** (Pseudomonas in 50-65%) is treated **topically**: ear toilet, antibiotic drops and keeping the ear dry; systemic antibiotics are added only in severe cases (slide p16). When the canal is too oedematous for drops to penetrate, an **ear wick** carries them along the whole canal. Because the drum cannot be seen, use a **quinolone** and avoid potentially ototoxic aminoglycoside drops.
w: Wrong - oral antibiotics are for severe or spreading disease; amoxicillin also misses Pseudomonas.
Wrong - syringing an acutely inflamed canal is painful and contraindicated in acute otitis externa.
Correct - after toilet, a wick lets topical quinolone reach a canal too swollen for drops alone.
Wrong - aminoglycosides are avoided when the drum is not seen, as a perforation risks ototoxicity.
Wrong - a young, non-diabetic patient without red flags does not need imaging.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old woman has had an itchy, blocked right ear for a month. She has used ciprofloxacin ear drops from a pharmacy for 3 weeks without improvement. Otoscopy shows moist grey-white debris studded with black dots, like wet newspaper, filling the canal. Once cleaned, the drum is intact.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Ear toilet, then topical clotrimazole 1% for two weeks
A further three-week course of ciprofloxacin ear drops
Oral flucloxacillin plus hydrocortisone-neomycin drops
Syringing three times a week with no topical medicine
Oral co-amoxiclav and a steroid-only drop for the itch
mcq.e: Itch and blockage with black spores (**Aspergillus niger**) or white debris (**Candida**) is **otomycosis**, often triggered by prolonged antibiotic drops that suppress the normal canal flora. Treat with meticulous **ear toilet** plus a topical **antifungal** such as clotrimazole and keep the ear dry (slide p17). More antibiotic or steroid drops feed the fungus; oral antifungals are reserved for immunocompromised or invasive cases.
w: Correct - remove the fungal mass, then apply a topical antifungal.
Wrong - prolonged antibiotic drops are the likely cause of the fungal overgrowth.
Wrong - antibacterial and steroid drops do not treat fungus and encourage it.
Wrong - repeated syringing keeps the canal moist and leaves the fungus untreated.
Wrong - systemic antibiotics and steroid drops promote fungal growth.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old office worker has had three episodes of diffuse otitis externa this year; the latest has just resolved with drops. He showers twice a day, swims weekly, cleans his ears after every shower and wears in-ear earbuds for several hours a day at work.
Which advice will best reduce recurrence?
o: Dry the canals with a cotton bud after every shower and swim
Wear the in-ear earbuds while showering to keep water out
Irrigate the canals weekly with warm tap water at home
Plug the ears with oil-soaked cotton when bathing; avoid swimming
Use his antibiotic ear drops twice weekly as prevention
mcq.e: Recurrent otitis externa is driven by **moisture** and **trauma** to the thin canal skin, which strips the protective wax layer. **Ear care advice** (slide p64): water precautions with an ear plug or **oil-soaked cotton wool** when bathing, avoid swimming, avoid washing inside the canal during ablution, no cotton buds or metal objects, limit prolonged earbud use and keep earbuds clean. Prophylactic antibiotic drops promote resistance and otomycosis.
w: Wrong - cotton buds traumatise the canal skin and remove protective wax.
Wrong - earbuds are not waterproof and their prolonged use is itself a risk factor.
Wrong - regular irrigation adds moisture and removes protective wax.
Correct - keeping water out (oil-soaked cotton or plug) and avoiding swimming protects the canal skin.
Wrong - prophylactic antibiotic drops encourage resistance and fungal infection.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 11%) has 6 weeks of right otalgia that keeps him awake at night and a scanty discharge despite two courses of antibiotic ear drops. Otoscopy shows granulation tissue on the floor of the canal at the bony-cartilaginous junction; the drum is intact. Cranial nerves are normal. ESR is 85 mm/h.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral co-amoxiclav and steroid ear drops, review in 2 weeks
Admit for IV ciprofloxacin, glucose control and biopsy
Cauterise the granulation in clinic and continue the drops
Urgent radical mastoidectomy to clear the infected bone
Oral fluconazole for 4 weeks with clotrimazole ear drops
mcq.e: An elderly diabetic with **nocturnal pain**, failure of topical treatment and **granulation on the canal floor** has **malignant (necrotising) otitis externa** until proven otherwise: a Pseudomonas osteomyelitis spreading to the skull base. Admit for pain and sugar control, give systemic anti-pseudomonal **ciprofloxacin** (IV for about 2 weeks, then oral, roughly 6-8 weeks in total), regular ear toilet, and **biopsy the granulation** to exclude carcinoma (slides p20-21). Antibiotics, not surgery, are the mainstay.
w: Wrong - outpatient co-amoxiclav does not cover Pseudomonas and steroid drops worsen infection.
Correct - admit, IV anti-pseudomonal therapy, tight sugar control, ear toilet and biopsy to exclude carcinoma.
Wrong - cautery leaves the underlying osteomyelitis untreated and misses a possible carcinoma.
Wrong - surgery is limited to biopsy or debridement; radical mastoidectomy is not the treatment.
Wrong - fungal skull-base infection is rare; Pseudomonas is the usual organism.

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old woman with diabetes is in week 5 of ciprofloxacin for a skull-base osteomyelitis that began in the left ear canal. Her night pain has gone, the canal is healing and her CRP has normalised. A technetium-99m bone scan at diagnosis was strongly positive. The team must decide whether antibiotics can be stopped.
Which investigation best guides that decision?
o: Repeat technetium-99m bone scan
Plain radiograph of both mastoids
Repeat ear swab for culture
High-resolution CT of temporal bone
Gallium-67 citrate scintigraphy
mcq.e: **Technetium-99m** reflects osteoblastic activity: it is sensitive for **diagnosis** but stays positive for months after infection is controlled, so it cannot show cure. **Gallium-67** (or an indium-labelled white cell scan) reflects active inflammation and normalises as infection settles, so with ESR/CRP and symptoms it is used to **monitor** response and decide when to stop. Note: slide p20 says the bone scan is for diagnosis and to evaluate response; correct is Tc-99m for diagnosis and gallium for monitoring (as slide p21 says).
w: Wrong - Tc-99m stays positive long after cure because bone remodelling continues.
Wrong - plain films are insensitive and do not reflect current infection activity.
Wrong - a healed canal may grow nothing, which says nothing about bone infection.
Wrong - CT shows bone erosion but changes lag and do not normalise with cure.
Correct - gallium uptake falls as inflammation resolves, so it guides when to stop antibiotics.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old man with diabetes has severe right ear pain, canal oedema, purulent exudate and granulation tissue on the canal floor. He has used ciprofloxacin drops for only 4 days. Applying the Cohen and Friedman (1987) criteria, the team notes that one major criterion is still missing.
Which finding would complete the major criteria?
o: Pseudomonas aeruginosa grown on ear swab
Raised ESR of 90 mm/h on admission bloods
Ipsilateral lower motor neurone facial palsy
Positive technetium-99m bone scan
Advanced age with poorly controlled diabetes
mcq.e: The Cohen and Friedman **major** criteria (all required) are pain, oedema, exudate, granulation tissue, microabscess at operation, and a **positive Tc-99m bone scan or failure of local treatment for at least 1 week**. Pseudomonas, cranial nerve involvement, diabetes, old age or debility and a positive bone radiograph are **minor** criteria that support but do not make the diagnosis. Note: slide p19 lists a high ESR as a criterion; it is not in the original criteria - ESR/CRP are used to monitor treatment.
w: Wrong - Pseudomonas on culture is a minor criterion.
Wrong - ESR is not part of the original Cohen criteria; it is used for monitoring.
Wrong - cranial nerve involvement is a minor criterion.
Correct - with only 4 days of drops, a positive Tc-99m scan supplies the remaining major criterion.
Wrong - diabetes and old age are minor criteria.

mcq.stem:
A 48-year-old Chinese man from Sibu has had 2 months of left ear blockage and muffled hearing. He has no otalgia, discharge or recent cold. Otoscopy shows a dull, retracted left drum with an air-fluid level; the right ear is normal. Tuning forks: Rinne negative on the left, Weber lateralises to the left.
What is the most important next step?
o: Endoscopic examination of the postnasal space
Left myringotomy with grommet insertion today
Two-week course of oral co-amoxiclav
Intranasal steroid spray and review in 3 months
MRI of the internal acoustic meatus
mcq.e: A **unilateral middle ear effusion in an adult**, especially of southern Chinese ethnicity in Malaysia, is **nasopharyngeal carcinoma** until proven otherwise: a tumour in the fossa of Rosenmüller blocks the Eustachian tube orifice (slide p23 lists nasopharyngeal mass). The next step is **nasoendoscopy** of the postnasal space with biopsy of any lesion, plus neck examination and EBV serology, before any grommet. Sprays or antibiotics only delay diagnosis of a curable cancer.
w: Correct - look at the nasopharynx first to exclude nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
Wrong - a grommet relieves the symptom but misses the cause; scope the nasopharynx first.
Wrong - antibiotics do not clear effusion and delay the essential examination.
Wrong - watchful waiting is for children; an adult with unilateral effusion needs the postnasal space examined.
Wrong - MRI IAM investigates asymmetric sensorineural loss; this is conductive.

mcq.stem:
A 5-year-old girl is referred because her kindergarten teacher thinks she ignores instructions and her speech lags behind her peers. She has had no ear pain or fever. Both drums are dull and yellowish with a diffuse light reflex and visible air bubbles; they are neither red nor perforated.
Which tympanometry result is most likely?
o: Type A, peak 0 daPa, ECV 0.9 ml
Type B, flat trace, ECV 4.5 ml
Type B, flat trace, ECV 0.8 ml
Type B, flat trace, ECV 0.1 ml
Type Ad, peak 0 daPa, ECV 0.9 ml
mcq.e: Fluid in the middle ear stops the drum moving at any pressure, giving a flat **Type B** trace; the **ear canal volume is normal** because the probe is measuring a normal canal against an intact drum (slide p26). A flat trace with a **high ECV** means a perforation or patent grommet, and a **low ECV** means wax or the probe against the canal wall. PTA will show a conductive loss.
w: Wrong - Type A means normal middle ear pressure and compliance, not a fluid-filled ear.
Wrong - a high ECV with a flat trace indicates a perforation or patent grommet; these drums are intact.
Correct - effusion behind an intact drum gives a flat trace with a normal canal volume.
Wrong - a very low ECV suggests occluding wax or the probe against the canal wall.
Wrong - Type Ad (hypermobile) suggests ossicular discontinuity or a flaccid drum.

mcq.stem:
A 4-year-old boy is reviewed in the ENT clinic 3 weeks after an episode of acute otitis media. He is well, with no pain. Both drums are dull with fluid levels. Tympanograms are Type B with normal ECV bilaterally and play audiometry shows a mild conductive loss of about 20 dB. His speech and behaviour are normal and he has no cleft palate or Down syndrome.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Bilateral myringotomy and grommet insertion now
Active observation with repeat tests at 3 months
Three weeks of oral amoxicillin to clear the fluid
Adenoidectomy alone on the next available list
Oral antihistamine and decongestant for a month
mcq.e: Most effusions, especially after AOM, clear spontaneously within 3 months, so the first step is **active observation** with repeat otoscopy, tympanometry and hearing tests (slide p27). Surgery is for **persistent OME beyond 3 months with a conductive loss over 25 dB**, or earlier when speech, development or structural risks (cleft palate, Down syndrome) demand it. Antibiotics, antihistamines and decongestants do not speed resolution; medical treatment (antihistamine, intranasal steroid) is only for children with allergic symptoms.
w: Wrong - grommets are for effusion persisting beyond 3 months with a loss over 25 dB.
Correct - most post-AOM effusions resolve within 3 months; observe actively and retest.
Wrong - antibiotics do not resolve OME and add side effects and resistance.
Wrong - there is no persistent effusion or adenoid symptom to justify surgery yet.
Wrong - no allergic symptoms; decongestants and antihistamines do not clear OME.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old boy has had bilateral middle ear effusions for 5 months despite watchful waiting. He snores loudly, breathes through his mouth and has a hyponasal voice. PTA shows a bilateral 35 dB conductive loss and both tympanograms are Type B with normal ECV. A lateral soft-tissue neck X-ray shows a large adenoid shadow.
Which procedure is most appropriate?
o: Bilateral myringotomy and grommets alone
Adenotonsillectomy without any ear surgery
Bilateral myringotomy with aspiration alone
Bilateral myringoplasty and adenoidectomy
Bilateral grommets with an adenoidectomy
mcq.e: Persistent OME **beyond 3 months with a conductive loss over 25 dB** is an indication for myringotomy and **grommet** (ventilation tube) insertion; because **adenoid hypertrophy** is obstructing the Eustachian tube orifices, **adenoidectomy** is added (slide p27). The grommet takes over ventilation of the middle ear; a myringotomy alone heals within days and the fluid returns. Myringoplasty repairs a perforation and has no role here.
w: Wrong - grommets alone leave the obstructing adenoid, so recurrence after extrusion is more likely.
Wrong - removing the adenoid without ventilating the ears leaves the current hearing loss untreated.
Wrong - a myringotomy closes within days, so the effusion re-accumulates.
Wrong - myringoplasty closes a perforation; these drums are intact.
Correct - ventilate the ears with grommets and remove the adenoid that blocks the Eustachian tubes.

mcq.stem:
In theatre, a registrar is about to insert a grommet in a 5-year-old with a middle ear effusion persisting for 4 months and a 30 dB conductive loss. Under the microscope the whole drum is visible after a little wax is removed. The consultant asks where the radial myringotomy should be made.
Which site is preferred?
o: Anteroinferior quadrant of the pars tensa
Posterosuperior quadrant of the pars tensa
Pars flaccida, just above the lateral process
Anterosuperior quadrant of the pars tensa
Directly over the umbo and handle of malleus
mcq.e: The **anteroinferior quadrant** is used (slide p27) because it lies away from the incus, stapes, chorda tympani and round window niche, which sit posteriorly, and it is easy to see. Grommets placed here also tend to stay in longer. The **pars flaccida** is the attic region, where retraction pockets and cholesteatoma arise, and the malleus handle is attached to the drum and must not be incised.
w: Correct - the safest and most visible site, clear of the ossicles and chorda tympani.
Wrong - the incus, stapes and chorda tympani lie behind this quadrant.
Wrong - the attic is not used for ventilation tubes and lies over the malleus neck and ossicular heads.
Wrong - the malleus handle and anterior malleal fold lie close by; this is not the standard site.
Wrong - the malleus is attached here; incising over it risks ossicular injury.

mcq.stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the ED at night after 2 days of a runny nose. He is crying inconsolably, pulling his right ear and has a temperature of 39.2 °C. The right drum is red, thickened and bulging with loss of landmarks; there is no discharge or perforation.
Which stage of the disease is this?
o: Stage of tubal occlusion
Stage of pre-suppuration
Stage of suppuration
Stage of resolution
Stage of complication
mcq.e: Pus forming under pressure in the middle ear pushes the drum outwards (**bulging**), so pain and fever are at their worst: the **stage of suppuration** (slide p33). **Tubal occlusion** gives a retracted drum; **pre-suppuration** gives a congested, hyperaemic drum without bulging; **resolution** follows rupture of the drum, when discharge appears and pain eases. This is the stage at which myringotomy relieves pain.
w: Wrong - tubal occlusion causes a retracted drum with mild symptoms.
Wrong - pre-suppuration shows a congested, hyperaemic drum but no bulging pus.
Correct - pus under pressure bulges the drum and pain and fever peak.
Wrong - resolution follows perforation, with discharge and easing pain.
Wrong - nothing here suggests mastoiditis or intracranial spread.

mcq.stem:
A 4-year-old girl had severe left earache and fever overnight. This morning the pain suddenly eased and her pillow was stained with blood-tinged pus. The canal contains mucopurulent discharge; after mopping, a small perforation is seen in the pars tensa. She has started oral amoxicillin.
Which ear drop is most appropriate to add?
o: Gentamicin-hydrocortisone ear drops
Ofloxacin 0.3% ear drops twice daily
Neomycin-polymyxin B-dexamethasone drops
Clotrimazole 1% ear solution
Chlorhexidine in alcohol ear drops
mcq.e: Sudden relief of pain with discharge marks the **stage of resolution**: the drum has ruptured and released the pus. Continue analgesia and oral amoxicillin; with a perforation, topical drops should be a **non-ototoxic quinolone** such as **ofloxacin** (slide p36). Aminoglycoside drops (gentamicin, neomycin) risk cochlear damage through a perforation, and alcohol solutions sting and are ototoxic.
w: Wrong - gentamicin is an aminoglycoside, ototoxic through a perforation.
Correct - a quinolone covers the pathogens without ototoxicity through the perforation.
Wrong - neomycin is an aminoglycoside and potentially ototoxic.
Wrong - an antifungal is for otomycosis, not bacterial AOM.
Wrong - alcohol and chlorhexidine are ototoxic and painful on middle ear mucosa.

mcq.stem:
A 3-year-old girl presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 2 days of right earache, fever of 38.8 °C and a cold. The right drum is red and bulging with no discharge. She has no drug allergies and is otherwise well. The medical officer writes a prescription.
Which regimen is most appropriate?
o: Oral chlorphenamine and pseudoephedrine with paracetamol
Ciprofloxacin ear drops plus an oral decongestant
Oral azithromycin with an oral antihistamine syrup
Oral amoxicillin for 5-7 days with regular paracetamol
Oral prednisolone with ibuprofen for pain and fever
mcq.e: **Amoxicillin** is the first-line antibiotic for AOM (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella), with regular **analgesia**; watchful waiting is an option in selected older children with mild illness. Antihistamines and decongestants do not shorten AOM or prevent complications and cause side effects in young children. Note: slide p36 lists an antihistamine for AOM with URTI; this has no proven benefit. Ear drops are for a perforated, discharging ear, and macrolides are for penicillin allergy.
w: Wrong - antihistamines and decongestants have no proven benefit in AOM and no antibiotic is given.
Wrong - drops cannot pass an intact drum; they are for a perforated ear.
Wrong - macrolides are second line, for penicillin allergy; the antihistamine adds nothing.
Correct - amoxicillin plus analgesia is first-line treatment for AOM.
Wrong - systemic steroids have no role in uncomplicated AOM.

mcq.stem:
