A 6-year-old boy has had severe right earache for 3 days despite 48 hours of oral amoxicillin and regular paracetamol. He is distressed and febrile. The right drum is red and markedly bulging with no perforation. There is no postauricular swelling, facial weakness or neck stiffness.
Which procedure gives the quickest relief of his pain?
o: Myringotomy of the bulging drum
Cortical (Schwartze) mastoidectomy
Adenoidectomy under anaesthesia
Myringoplasty with temporalis graft
Aural toilet and ear wick insertion
mcq.e: **Myringotomy** releases pus under pressure through an incision in the drum, giving immediate relief of pain and a sample for culture; it is indicated for **severe pain with a bulging drum** or failure of antibiotics (slide p36). Without signs of mastoiditis or intracranial spread, mastoidectomy is not needed, though the antibiotic may be changed to co-amoxiclav. Myringoplasty repairs perforations and an ear wick is used in otitis externa.
w: Correct - draining the pus decompresses the middle ear and relieves pain at once.
Wrong - mastoidectomy is for complications such as mastoid abscess; none are present.
Wrong - adenoidectomy may reduce recurrent episodes but does not relieve this acute pain.
Wrong - myringoplasty repairs a chronic perforation; the drum here is intact.
Wrong - an ear wick is for a swollen canal in otitis externa, not pus behind the drum.

mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old woman has had intermittent left ear discharge for 2 years, worse after colds and when water enters the ear. The discharge is copious, mucoid and does not smell. Otoscopy shows a large kidney-shaped hole in the pars tensa with a rim of drum all round; the attic is intact and there is no keratin.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Atticoantral (squamous) chronic otitis media
Acute otitis media in the stage of resolution
Otomycosis with a secondary drum perforation
Chronic otitis externa with granular myringitis
Tubotympanic (mucosal) chronic otitis media
mcq.e: Profuse, mucoid, odourless discharge from a **central perforation** (rim present all round) is **tubotympanic or 'safe' COM** (slide p38): disease is confined to the mucosa, cholesteatoma is absent and complications are rare. The discharge is mucoid and profuse because it comes from the goblet cells of the middle ear mucosa. Symptoms for longer than 3 months exclude AOM (under 3 weeks).
w: Wrong - atticoantral disease gives a marginal or attic perforation with scanty, foul discharge.
Wrong - AOM lasts under 3 weeks; this has been present for 2 years.
Wrong - otomycosis causes itch and fungal debris, not a mucoid discharge through a central perforation.
Wrong - otitis externa produces canal and drum surface inflammation, not a mucoid middle ear discharge.
Correct - central perforation with profuse, odourless mucoid discharge is the safe mucosal type.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old farmer has had right ear discharge on and off for 18 months with reduced hearing. He is referred from a Klinik Kesihatan, where only pus in the canal could be seen. In the ENT clinic the ear is mopped and examined under the microscope.
Which finding would most indicate disease with a high risk of complications?
o: Central perforation with mucoid discharge
Attic perforation with scanty, foul discharge
Dry central perforation with tympanosclerosis
Retracted intact drum with an air-fluid level
Diffuse canal oedema with tragal tenderness
mcq.e: **Atticoantral (unsafe) COM** involves the attic and antrum: the perforation is **marginal or in the pars flaccida**, and the discharge is **scanty but foul** from bone destruction and anaerobes (slide p38). **Cholesteatoma** and granulation are common and erode bone, so complications (labyrinthine fistula, facial palsy, intracranial sepsis) are frequent. A central perforation with profuse mucoid discharge suggests safe tubotympanic disease.
w: Wrong - central perforation with mucoid discharge is the safe tubotympanic pattern.
Correct - attic or marginal perforation with scanty, foul discharge signals unsafe disease and likely cholesteatoma.
Wrong - an inactive dry perforation carries a low risk of complications.
Wrong - this describes middle ear effusion behind an intact drum.
Wrong - these are signs of otitis externa, not of middle ear disease.

mcq.stem:
A 9-year-old boy with long-standing left ear discharge has 5 days of fever and worsening pain. The left pinna is pushed forwards and downwards. Behind it there is a tender, fluctuant, red swelling that obliterates the retroauricular groove. Otoscopy shows pus and sagging of the posterosuperior canal wall.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Postauricular reactive lymphadenitis
Furunculosis of the posterior canal wall
Acute mastoiditis with mastoid abscess
Bezold abscess deep to sternomastoid
Perichondritis of the pinna and concha
mcq.e: Pus breaking through the mastoid cortex lifts the periosteum behind the ear, pushing the **pinna forwards and downwards** and obliterating the retroauricular groove; **sagging of the posterosuperior meatal wall** (the bone over the antrum) is the key otoscopic sign (slide p40). Lymphadenitis and furunculosis can also push the pinna forwards, but the groove is preserved and the meatal wall does not sag. Manage with admission, IV antibiotics, HRCT and **cortical mastoidectomy**.
w: Wrong - lymphadenitis leaves the retroauricular groove intact and the meatal wall normal.
Wrong - a furuncle is a localised canal swelling; it does not cause sagging of the bony posterosuperior wall.
Correct - pinna displaced forwards and downwards plus posterosuperior meatal sagging is a mastoid abscess.
Wrong - a Bezold abscess lies in the neck below the mastoid tip, not behind the pinna.
Wrong - perichondritis inflames the pinna itself and does not affect the canal wall.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man with untreated foul-smelling right ear discharge for years presents with fever and a painful, firm swelling in the upper right neck. The swelling lies deep to the sternocleidomastoid below the mastoid tip, and he holds his head tilted to the right. The pinna is in a normal position with no swelling above or in front of the ear.
Which abscess is this?
o: Bezold abscess
Citelli abscess
Luc abscess
Zygomatic abscess
Postauricular abscess
mcq.e: When pus breaks through the **medial side of the mastoid tip** it tracks along the sternocleidomastoid to form a **Bezold abscess**, deep to the muscle in the upper neck (slides p39-43). A **Citelli** abscess follows the posterior belly of digastric into the digastric triangle; a **Luc** abscess passes through the roof of the canal to lie deep to temporalis; a **zygomatic** abscess lies above and in front of the ear. Treat with IV antibiotics, drainage and mastoidectomy.
w: Correct - pus from the mastoid tip tracking deep to the sternocleidomastoid is a Bezold abscess.
Wrong - a Citelli abscess lies in the digastric triangle along the posterior belly of digastric.
Wrong - a Luc abscess lies deep to temporalis, above the ear, via the canal roof.
Wrong - a zygomatic abscess lies in front of and above the pinna.
Wrong - a postauricular abscess lies behind the pinna and pushes it forwards and downwards.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old woman with chronic left ear discharge develops deep pain behind the left eye and double vision on looking to the left. Examination shows foul pus in the left canal and failure of abduction of the left eye; other cranial nerves are normal and she is alert without neck stiffness.
Where has the infection most likely spread?
o: Sigmoid (lateral) venous sinus
Lateral semicircular canal
Mastoid tip with a neck collection
Petrous apex of the temporal bone
Cavernous sinus via ophthalmic veins
mcq.e: Persistent **otorrhoea**, **retro-orbital (trigeminal) pain** and **lateral rectus (VI) palsy** form **Gradenigo syndrome**, from petrositis (slide p41). The abducens nerve crosses the petrous apex in Dorello's canal and the trigeminal ganglion lies on its anterior surface, so both are irritated. Confirm with CT/MRI and treat with IV antibiotics and mastoid surgery.
w: Wrong - sigmoid sinus thrombophlebitis causes picket-fence fever, not an isolated VI palsy.
Wrong - a labyrinthine fistula causes vertigo and hearing loss, not diplopia.
Wrong - a neck collection (Bezold) does not involve cranial nerves V and VI.
Correct - petrous apex infection irritates the VI nerve and trigeminal ganglion: Gradenigo syndrome.
Wrong - cavernous sinus thrombosis gives proptosis, chemosis and multiple ocular nerve palsies.

mcq.stem:
A 16-year-old with foul-smelling left ear discharge for years is admitted with headache and high spiking fevers with rigors twice daily, the temperature falling to normal in between. There is tender oedema over the posterior part of the left mastoid. He is alert, with no neck stiffness or focal neurological signs. Blood cultures are pending.
Which complication is most likely?
o: Otogenic temporal lobe abscess
Lateral sinus thrombophlebitis
Extradural abscess over the tegmen
Otitic bacterial meningitis
Subdural empyema over the convexity
mcq.e: **Picket-fence fever** with rigors (septic emboli shed from an infected thrombus) and oedema over the mastoid emissary vein (**Griesinger sign**) indicate **lateral (sigmoid) sinus thrombophlebitis**, an intracranial complication of COM (slide p39). Meningitis gives neck stiffness and photophobia, and a brain abscess or empyema gives focal signs and raised pressure. Confirm with contrast CT or MR venography; treat with IV antibiotics and mastoidectomy with exposure of the sinus.
w: Wrong - a temporal lobe abscess gives raised pressure and focal signs such as dysphasia.
Correct - picket-fence fever plus Griesinger sign points to an infected sigmoid sinus thrombus.
Wrong - an extradural abscess is often silent or causes local headache, not swinging rigors.
Wrong - meningitis gives neck stiffness and photophobia, absent here.
Wrong - a subdural empyema causes rapid deterioration with seizures and focal deficits.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old man has a central perforation of the right drum that has stayed dry for 8 months with water precautions. There is no keratin or attic retraction. PTA shows a 25 dB conductive loss on the right with normal bone conduction. He wants to be able to swim again.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Cortical (Schwartze) mastoidectomy
Modified radical mastoidectomy
Myringoplasty with a fascia graft
Myringotomy and grommet insertion
Bone-anchored hearing aid fitting
mcq.e: This is **inactive mucosal COM**: a dry perforation. Keep the ear dry, record hearing with an audiogram and, once the ear has been **dry for about 6 months**, offer **myringoplasty** (repair of the drum, usually with a temporalis fascia graft) to restore hearing and allow water exposure (slide p44). Mastoidectomy is for complicated active disease or cholesteatoma, and a grommet treats effusion behind an intact drum.
w: Wrong - cortical mastoidectomy is for active disease with complications such as mastoiditis.
Wrong - a canal wall down operation is for cholesteatoma, not a dry mucosal perforation.
Correct - a dry perforation for over 6 months is ready for myringoplasty.
Wrong - a grommet ventilates an intact drum; this drum already has a hole.
Wrong - repairing the drum can restore hearing; an implant is not the first option.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old woman has had right ear discharge for 4 months. The discharge is mucopurulent; after mopping there is a central perforation with inflamed but non-granular mucosa and no keratin. She has no vertigo, facial weakness, headache or fever. This is her first treatment.
What is the best initial management?
o: Pus swab, withholding treatment until culture returns
Oral amoxicillin for 2 weeks without any ear drops
Urgent HRCT temporal bone and cortical mastoidectomy
Gentamicin ear drops with weekly ear syringing
Aural toilet, ofloxacin drops and keeping the ear dry
mcq.e: **Active COM without complication** is treated in clinic: **aural toilet** so drops reach the mucosa, **topical ofloxacin** (better than oral antibiotics because it reaches high local concentrations and is not ototoxic) and strict **dry-ear precautions** (slide p45). A swab is reserved for cases that fail to resolve, and systemic antibiotics are added for children, granulation tissue or failed topical treatment. HRCT and mastoidectomy are for complicated disease.
w: Wrong - a swab is for unresolved cases; treatment should not be delayed.
Wrong - topical drops after ear toilet work better than oral antibiotics.
Wrong - imaging and surgery are for complications, which are absent here.
Wrong - gentamicin is ototoxic through a perforation and syringing a perforated ear is contraindicated.
Correct - clean, give topical quinolone and keep dry; observe for complications.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old boy is referred from Klinik Kesihatan after a school hearing screen. Otoscopy of the right ear shows a smooth pearly-white mass behind the anterosuperior quadrant of an intact, mobile tympanic membrane; the pars tensa and pars flaccida look normal. His mother recalls two episodes of acute otitis media treated with oral amoxicillin, never with ear discharge.
Which additional history would make a congenital origin untenable under the Levenson criteria?
o: Myringotomy and grommet insertion in that ear at age 3
A third episode of acute otitis media treated last year
A 25 dB conductive hearing loss on that side on PTA
Mass seen in the anterosuperior rather than posterior quadrant
A family history of cholesteatoma in his father
mcq.e: **Levenson criteria** for congenital cholesteatoma: white mass medial to a **normal TM**, normal pars tensa and pars flaccida, **no history of otorrhoea or perforation**, and **no previous otological procedure**. A grommet is an otological procedure that breaches the drum and could implant squamous epithelium, so the lesion can no longer be called congenital. Previous AOM without otorrhoea is NOT an exclusion, because most children have had AOM.
w: Correct - a previous otological procedure (which also perforates the drum) excludes a congenital cholesteatoma under Levenson.
Wrong - AOM episodes without otorrhoea or perforation do not exclude it; almost every child has had AOM.
Wrong - a conductive loss is an expected effect of a middle ear mass, not an exclusion criterion.
Wrong - the anterosuperior quadrant is actually the classic site of congenital cholesteatoma.
Wrong - family history is not part of the Levenson criteria.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old man attends ENT clinic with a blocked left ear. Microscopy shows a retraction pocket of the pars flaccida draped onto the neck of the malleus, and the outer attic wall shows a small area of limited bony erosion. The base of the pocket is visible and dry, with no keratin.
Which grade best describes this retraction?
o: Tos grade 2
Tos grade 3
Tos grade 4
Sadé grade 3
Sadé grade 2
mcq.e: **Tos** grades the **pars flaccida**: 1 not touching the malleus neck, 2 touching the malleus neck, 3 as grade 2 plus **limited erosion of the scutum** (outer attic wall), 4 as grade 3 plus severe erosion. **Sadé** grades the **pars tensa** (1 slight retraction, 2 onto incus/stapes, 3 atelectasis onto promontory, 4 adhesive otitis). Any scutal erosion lifts a contact pocket from grade 2 to at least grade 3.
w: Wrong - grade 2 is contact with the malleus neck without any scutal erosion.
Correct - contact with the malleus neck plus limited scutum erosion is Tos grade 3.
Wrong - grade 4 needs severe erosion of the outer attic wall.
Wrong - Sadé grades describe the pars tensa (grade 3 = atelectasis onto the promontory), not attic pockets.
Wrong - Sadé grade 2 is a pars tensa retraction onto the incus or stapes.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old woman has 2 years of scanty, foul-smelling right otorrhoea. Microscopy shows a pars flaccida perforation with white keratin flakes. PTA shows a 35 dB conductive loss. HRCT temporal bone is requested to plan surgery.
Which CT finding is typically the earliest bony sign of this disease?
o: Erosion of the lateral semicircular canal bony capsule
Dehiscence of the tegmen tympani over the attic
Blunting of the scutum at the lateral attic wall
Opacification with sclerosis of the mastoid air cells
Erosion of the bony facial canal at the second genu
mcq.e: An attic (pars flaccida) cholesteatoma presses first against the **scutum**, the sharp bony spur of the lateral attic wall, so **blunting of the scutum is often the earliest CT sign**. The other HRCT hallmark is a well-defined homogeneous soft-tissue mass in the attic or non-dependent areas. Labyrinthine fistula, tegmen dehiscence and facial canal erosion are later complications to look for on the scan, not early signs.
w: Wrong - a lateral canal fistula is a later complication (circumscribed labyrinthitis).
Wrong - tegmen erosion is a later finding that warns of intracranial spread.
Correct - scutal blunting is the classic earliest bony sign of attic cholesteatoma.
Wrong - a sclerotic, opacified mastoid reflects long-standing chronic otitis media, not an early erosive sign.
Wrong - facial canal erosion is a later finding that risks facial palsy.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man is referred for myringoplasty with a note: 'dry central perforation, safe ear'. Under the microscope there is a dry central perforation of the right pars tensa. A small brown crust sits over the pars flaccida, and on direct questioning he admits occasional scanty, smelly discharge.
What is the best next step?
o: List for myringoplasty after 6 months of a dry ear
Topical ofloxacin drops for 2 weeks, then review
Repeat PTA and tympanometry before listing
Microsuction of the crust to inspect the attic
Ear swab for culture and sensitivity first
mcq.e: An attic cholesteatoma can coexist with a central perforation, so **always examine the attic even when a central perforation is seen**. A crust over the pars flaccida often hides an attic perforation or retraction pocket full of keratin, and scanty foul discharge is an unsafe-ear feature. If cholesteatoma is found, the plan changes from myringoplasty to mastoid surgery with HRCT.
w: Wrong - listing for myringoplasty risks closing the drum over an undiagnosed attic cholesteatoma.
Wrong - drops do not answer the key question of what lies under the attic crust.
Wrong - hearing tests are needed later but will not exclude cholesteatoma.
Correct - clear the crust under the microscope and inspect the pars flaccida for a cholesteatoma sac.
Wrong - a swab is for unresolved active discharge and does not examine the attic.

mcq.stem:
A 42-year-old teacher has extensive cholesteatoma filling the attic and antrum of her left ear. Bone conduction is normal and at surgery the stapes is intact and mobile. The surgeon decides the posterior canal wall must be taken down for safe clearance, but wants to keep her chance of useful hearing.
Which procedure is most appropriate?
o: Radical mastoidectomy
Cortical (Schwartz) mastoidectomy
Combined approach tympanoplasty
Atticotomy alone
Modified radical mastoidectomy
mcq.e: Both radical and **modified radical mastoidectomy (MRM)** are **canal wall down**: the posterior meatal wall is removed and the middle ear, attic, antrum and mastoid become one cavity. Radical mastoidectomy removes the TM remnants and ossicles (except the stapes footplate) and obliterates the Eustachian tube, so no hearing mechanism is left. MRM **preserves the TM remnant and ossicular remnants (handle of malleus, stapes)** and can be combined with tympanoplasty to rebuild hearing.
w: Wrong - radical mastoidectomy clears disease but removes the hearing mechanism and blocks the Eustachian tube.
Wrong - cortical mastoidectomy is canal wall up and is used for acute mastoiditis, not extensive cholesteatoma.
Wrong - combined approach tympanoplasty keeps the posterior canal wall (canal wall up).
Wrong - atticotomy alone is a limited canal wall up procedure for small attic disease.
Correct - MRM takes down the canal wall but preserves the drum remnant and ossicles for hearing.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old man with no past ear infections or perforation develops a keratin-filled sac in the attic. Histology of the excised pars flaccida shows the basal layer of its squamous epithelium proliferating and breaking through the basement membrane into the subepithelial connective tissue.
Which theory of cholesteatoma formation does this histology support?
o: Basal cell hyperplasia with papillary ingrowth (Ruedi)
Invagination of a retraction pocket (Wittmaack)
Epithelial migration through a perforation (Habermann)
Squamous metaplasia of middle ear mucosa (Sadé)
Embryonic epidermoid cell rest (Michaels)
mcq.e: **Ruedi's basal cell hyperplasia** theory: basal cells of the pars flaccida proliferate and push papillary cones through the basement membrane, and these become cholesteatoma behind an intact drum. With **Wittmaack's invagination** theory, standard texts (Dhingra) class it as **primary acquired** (no prior perforation or infection). Habermann's migration and Sadé's metaplasia need a perforation or infected mucosa, so they explain **secondary acquired** disease. Note: slide p51 lists Ruedi under secondary acquired; most texts place it under primary acquired.
w: Correct - basal layer proliferation through the basement membrane is Ruedi's theory (primary acquired).
Wrong - Wittmaack explains a deepening retraction pocket, not basal layer invasion on histology.
Wrong - Habermann requires a perforation for canal skin to migrate in; he has never had one.
Wrong - Sadé's metaplasia follows chronic infection of middle ear mucosa, which he has not had.
Wrong - an embryonic cell rest explains congenital cholesteatoma, not a pars flaccida lesion in an adult.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man with long-standing foul-smelling left otorrhoea complains of brief spinning when he presses on his left tragus or blows his nose. Microscopy shows an attic perforation filled with keratin. Pressing the tragus to raise canal pressure produces vertigo and nystagmus.
Which structure has most likely been eroded?
o: Posterior semicircular canal
Lateral semicircular canal
Superior semicircular canal
Cochlear promontory
Stapes footplate at oval window
mcq.e: A **positive fistula test** means pressure in the canal is being transmitted to the labyrinth through eroded bone (**circumscribed labyrinthitis**, slide p77). The **lateral (horizontal) semicircular canal** bulges into the medial wall of the aditus and antrum, directly in the path of attic-antral cholesteatoma, so it is the commonest fistula site. Confirm with HRCT and plan surgery; the matrix over a fistula is handled carefully to protect hearing.
w: Wrong - the posterior canal lies deep in the petrous bone, away from the antrum, and is rarely eroded.
Correct - the lateral canal prominence faces the aditus and antrum and is the commonest fistula site.
Wrong - superior canal dehiscence is usually a non-infective thinning of the middle fossa floor.
Wrong - promontory erosion is uncommon and would threaten the cochlea rather than the canal.
Wrong - the footplate is a rare fistula site compared with the lateral canal.

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old man attends Klinik Kesihatan with 'dizziness' for 3 weeks. He feels light-headed and his vision greys out within seconds of getting up from a chair; there is no spinning, no hearing loss and no tinnitus. Amlodipine and a thiazide were started last month. Ear and neurological examinations are normal.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Dix-Hallpike test on both sides
Pure tone audiometry and tympanometry
Lying and standing blood pressure
Oral betahistine and review in 2 weeks
MRI internal acoustic meatus
mcq.e: Vertigo is a symptom, so first decide whether it is **true vertigo** (an illusion of rotation) or **light-headedness/presyncope** or imbalance. Greying out on standing with no spinning, after new antihypertensives, points to **postural hypotension**, so measure lying and standing BP. Vestibular tests and betahistine are for true rotatory vertigo.
w: Wrong - Dix-Hallpike tests for BPPV, which causes spinning on lying down or rolling over, not presyncope on standing.
Wrong - audiometry is for hearing symptoms or true vertigo; he has neither.
Correct - presyncope on standing after new antihypertensives calls for a postural BP check.
Wrong - betahistine is for Ménière's-type vertigo and would not help postural hypotension.
Wrong - imaging of the IAM is for asymmetrical hearing loss or unilateral tinnitus.

mcq.stem:
A 48-year-old lift technician had a head injury 2 months ago. He now reports an exaggerated sinking or rising sensation whenever the lift starts moving up or down, but no spinning when turning his head and no hearing loss. Dix-Hallpike testing is negative.
Dysfunction of which vestibular end-organ best explains his symptom?
o: Utricle
Lateral semicircular canal
Posterior semicircular canal
Saccule
Superior semicircular canal
mcq.e: The **semicircular canals** detect **angular** (rotational) acceleration; the **otolith organs** detect **linear** acceleration and gravity. The **utricle** senses horizontal linear movement (forwards and backwards); the **saccule** senses **vertical linear movement** (up and down, as in a lift). The trap is the utricle: it is the source of BPPV otoconia, but it senses horizontal, not vertical, movement.
w: Wrong - the utricle senses horizontal linear (forward-backward) acceleration.
Wrong - the lateral canal senses rotation in the horizontal plane, such as turning the head.
Wrong - the posterior canal senses rotation and is the canal involved in BPPV.
Correct - the saccule senses vertical linear acceleration, such as a lift starting up or down.
Wrong - the superior canal senses rotation (nodding), not linear movement.

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension presents to ED with sudden vertigo and vomiting for 6 hours. He cannot stand without support. There is vertical downbeating nystagmus that is unchanged with visual fixation, hearing is normal, and there is mild left finger-nose ataxia.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Epley manoeuvre and discharge home
IV prochlorperazine then discharge with betahistine
Vestibular rehabilitation exercises
Urgent pure tone audiometry next morning
Urgent brain imaging via the stroke pathway
mcq.e: Central features: **severe, constant imbalance**, **neurological signs**, and **vertical or direction-changing nystagmus not suppressed by visual fixation**, with slow recovery. Peripheral vertigo gives unidirectional horizontal-torsional nystagmus that is suppressed by fixation, fatigable, with latency, often with hearing loss. In a vascular-risk patient this is a posterior circulation (cerebellar) stroke until proven otherwise: the must-not-miss diagnosis.
w: Wrong - Epley treats BPPV; this nystagmus is constant and vertical, not positional.
Wrong - sedating and discharging a likely cerebellar stroke is a dangerous miss.
Wrong - rehabilitation is for compensated peripheral loss, not an acute central event.
Wrong - hearing is normal and audiometry does not address the stroke risk.
Correct - central signs with vascular risk factors need urgent brain imaging for posterior circulation stroke.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old woman has 2 weeks of brief spinning attacks when she rolls onto her right side in bed or looks up to a high shelf; each lasts under a minute. Hearing is normal. On right Dix-Hallpike testing, after a 5-second latency, there is upbeating torsional nystagmus with the upper pole beating towards the right (lower) ear, lasting 20 seconds and weaker on repetition.
What is the best management?
o: Epley manoeuvre for the right posterior canal
Barbecue (Lempert) roll for the lateral canal
Epley manoeuvre for the left posterior canal
Betahistine 16 mg three times daily for 3 months
Urgent MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging
mcq.e: This is posterior canal **BPPV**: otoconia dislodged from the **utricle** into the **posterior semicircular canal** (about 80% of cases). A positive Dix-Hallpike shows **latency of a few seconds, upbeating torsional geotropic nystagmus lasting under a minute, which fatigues**; the undermost ear is the affected one. Treat with canalith repositioning (**Epley**) starting on the affected side; drugs do not help. Note: slide p72 says attacks last seconds to minutes; classic BPPV attacks last under a minute.
w: Correct - a positive right Dix-Hallpike means right posterior canal BPPV, treated by a right-sided Epley.
Wrong - the barbecue roll is for lateral canal BPPV, which gives horizontal nystagmus on supine roll testing.
Wrong - the undermost (right) ear during the positive test is the affected side.
Wrong - betahistine has no role in BPPV; repositioning is curative in most patients.
Wrong - latency, fatigability and torsional geotropic nystagmus are classic peripheral BPPV, not central.

mcq.stem:
A 44-year-old woman has had four attacks over 6 months of spinning vertigo lasting 2-3 hours, with vomiting, a roaring left tinnitus and left ear fullness. Between attacks she is well. PTA during a recent attack showed left thresholds of 45 dB HL at 250 and 500 Hz and 20 dB HL from 2 to 8 kHz, with no air-bone gap; this improved a month later.
What is the underlying pathology?
o: Otoconia displaced into the posterior canal
Distension of the endolymphatic compartment
Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve
Schwannoma of the vestibular nerve in the IAM
Ischaemia in the anterior inferior cerebellar artery
mcq.e: Episodic vertigo lasting **20 minutes to hours** with **fluctuating low-frequency SNHL, tinnitus and aural fullness** is **Ménière's disease**, caused by idiopathic **endolymphatic hydrops** (distension of the endolymphatic space). BPPV lasts seconds, vestibular neuritis is a single attack lasting days without hearing loss, and a schwannoma causes progressive rather than fluctuating loss.
w: Wrong - BPPV attacks are positional, last seconds and spare hearing.
Correct - endolymphatic hydrops causes the triad with fluctuating low-frequency SNHL.
Wrong - vestibular neuritis is a single prolonged attack over days, with normal hearing.
Wrong - a vestibular schwannoma causes progressive asymmetrical loss, not discrete reversible attacks.
Wrong - an AICA stroke is a single sudden event with neurological signs, not recurrent reversible attacks.

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old man with a 4-year history of definite left-sided Ménière's disease still has two disabling attacks a month despite a low-salt diet, reduced caffeine and regular betahistine. His left ear now has a flat 75 dB HL sensorineural loss; the right ear is normal.
What is the most appropriate next treatment?
o: Daily prochlorperazine taken long term
Repeated Epley manoeuvres every month
Intratympanic gentamicin to the left ear
Endolymphatic sac surgery on the right
Vestibular rehabilitation as sole therapy
mcq.e: **Vestibular sedatives** (prochlorperazine, promethazine) are for **acute attacks only**, because long-term use delays central compensation. **Intratympanic gentamicin** is a chemical labyrinthectomy: it controls vertigo in most patients but can worsen hearing, so it suits an ear whose hearing is already poor. Surgery (endolymphatic sac decompression, vestibular neurectomy) is for failed medical treatment and is done on the affected side. Note: slide p76 lists betahistine (Betaserc) with the sedatives; it is a histamine analogue, not a vestibular sedative.
w: Wrong - long-term vestibular sedatives impair central compensation; use them only during attacks.
Wrong - Epley repositions otoconia in BPPV and has no role in hydrops.
Correct - with hearing already poor in the left ear, ablative intratympanic gentamicin is the logical next step.
Wrong - surgery would be done on the affected left ear, never the normal right ear.
Wrong - rehabilitation helps chronic imbalance but does not stop recurrent hydrops attacks.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old man with long-standing foul-smelling right otorrhoea presents to ED with 2 days of fever, severe constant vertigo and vomiting. PTA shows no response in the right ear at maximum output on both air and bone conduction. Horizontal nystagmus beats towards the left ear.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Serous (viral) labyrinthitis
Circumscribed labyrinthitis from a canal fistula
Vestibular neuritis
Suppurative labyrinthitis
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
mcq.e: **Suppurative labyrinthitis**: bacteria invade the labyrinth (from COM/cholesteatoma or meningitis), destroying it, so there is a **total, permanent SNHL (dead ear)**, severe vertigo and nystagmus beating towards the healthy ear. Serous labyrinthitis (toxins or virus) gives partial, recoverable hearing loss; a circumscribed fistula gives brief pressure-induced vertigo with hearing preserved. Admit for IV antibiotics and mastoid surgery, and watch for meningitis.
w: Wrong - serous labyrinthitis gives partial, often recoverable hearing loss, not a dead ear.
Wrong - a circumscribed fistula causes brief pressure-induced vertigo with hearing largely preserved.
Wrong - vestibular neuritis spares hearing and is not linked to chronic otorrhoea.
Correct - a dead ear with severe vertigo and fever in unsafe COM means bacterial invasion of the labyrinth.
Wrong - BPPV is brief, positional and never causes a dead ear.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old woman has 1 year of left-sided tinnitus and gradually worsening left hearing, with mild unsteadiness but no spinning attacks. Otoscopy is normal. PTA: right ear normal; left ear AC and BC equal at 15 dB HL at 250-500 Hz, 35 dB HL at 2 kHz and 45 dB HL at 4-8 kHz. Tympanometry is type A in both ears.
What is the most appropriate investigation?
o: HRCT temporal bone with fine bone cuts
Repeat PTA in 12 months to watch for progression
Dix-Hallpike test on the left side
Carotid and vertebral artery Doppler
Gadolinium MRI of internal acoustic meatus
mcq.e: **Asymmetrical SNHL or unilateral tinnitus** must be investigated to exclude a **vestibular schwannoma** (acoustic neuroma); the test of choice is **MRI of the internal acoustic meatus** (gadolinium-enhanced or high-resolution T2). HRCT shows bone, not a small nerve-sheath tumour. Note: slide p70 lists acoustic neuroma under central causes; it arises from the vestibular nerve in the IAM/cerebellopontine angle (retrocochlear) and gives central signs only when large.
w: Wrong - HRCT is for bony middle ear disease such as cholesteatoma and misses small intracanalicular tumours.
Wrong - waiting a year risks missing a growing tumour; asymmetry needs imaging now.
Wrong - she has no positional vertigo, so Dix-Hallpike adds nothing.
Wrong - vascular imaging does not explain a progressive unilateral SNHL.
Correct - gadolinium MRI of the IAM is the investigation of choice to exclude vestibular schwannoma.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old woman with a 20-year history of an intermittently discharging left ear attends ENT clinic. PTA of the left ear: air conduction 60, 65, 70 and 75 dB HL at 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 kHz; bone conduction 30, 35, 40 and 45 dB HL at the same frequencies. The right ear is normal.
How is the left-ear hearing loss best classified?
o: Moderate mixed hearing loss
Severe mixed hearing loss
Moderate conductive hearing loss
Moderate sensorineural hearing loss
Mild sensorineural hearing loss
mcq.e: **Severity** is read from the **air conduction** average (here about 68 dB HL = **moderate**, 41-70 dB HL on the BSA scale). **Type** is read from **bone conduction**: BC is abnormal (above 20 dB HL) and there is a 30 dB air-bone gap, so the loss is **mixed**, the classic pattern of chronic otitis media (conductive element from the perforation or ossicles plus cochlear damage from toxins). Note: slides p85 and p89 say an air-bone gap of 10 dB or more, p91 says more than 10 dB; teach a gap of more than about 10 dB.
w: Correct - AC average about 68 dB HL is moderate; abnormal BC plus a 30 dB gap makes it mixed.
Wrong - severe starts at 71 dB HL; the AC average here is about 68 dB HL.
Wrong - conductive loss needs normal BC; her BC is 30-45 dB HL.
Wrong - sensorineural loss has no air-bone gap; here the gap is 30 dB.
Wrong - mild is 20-40 dB HL, and the large air-bone gap excludes pure SNHL.

mcq.stem:
A 46-year-old man who has worked for 20 years in a palm-oil mill without ear protection finds it hard to follow conversation in crowded places. Otoscopy is normal. PTA in both ears: AC and BC equal, 15 dB HL from 250 Hz to 2 kHz, 55 dB HL at 4 kHz, and 30 dB HL at 8 kHz.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Age-related hearing loss (presbycusis)
Noise-induced hearing loss
Aminoglycoside ototoxicity
Otosclerosis with cochlear involvement
Bilateral Ménière's disease
mcq.e: A bilateral sensorineural **notch at 4 kHz with recovery at 8 kHz** is the signature of **noise-induced hearing loss**: the cochlear region tuned around 4 kHz is the most vulnerable to noise trauma. Presbycusis slopes down steadily to 8 kHz without recovery, ototoxicity starts at the highest frequencies, and Ménière's affects the low frequencies first. Advise hearing protection and workplace hearing surveillance.
w: Wrong - presbycusis gives a steadily sloping high-frequency loss that is worst at 8 kHz, with no recovery.
Correct - a 4 kHz notch recovering at 8 kHz in a noise-exposed worker is classic noise-induced loss.
Wrong - aminoglycoside damage begins at the highest frequencies (8 kHz and above).
Wrong - otosclerosis gives a conductive loss with an air-bone gap; here AC equals BC.
Wrong - Ménière's gives fluctuating low-frequency loss with vertigo, usually one-sided at first.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old woman notices that her hearing in both ears has worsened since her second pregnancy, yet she hears speech better on a noisy bus. Both tympanic membranes look normal. PTA shows bilateral AC thresholds around 45 dB HL across all frequencies; BC is 10-15 dB HL except for a dip to 35 dB HL at 2 kHz. Tympanograms show a peak at 0 daPa with compliance of 0.2 ml.
What is the most likely underlying pathology?
o: Fluid filling the middle ear cleft
Disruption of the incudostapedial joint
Otospongiotic fixation of the stapes
Hyaline plaques within the tympanic membrane
Outer hair cell loss at the basal cochlea
mcq.e: Progressive bilateral **conductive loss with a normal drum** in a young woman, worse with pregnancy, with paracusis Willisii (hearing better in noise), suggests **otosclerosis**. The **Carhart notch** (BC dip at **2 kHz**) is a mechanical artefact of stapes fixation that improves after stapes surgery, and the tympanogram is **type As** (normal pressure, low compliance). Effusion would give a flat type B trace, and ossicular discontinuity a high-compliance type Ad.
w: Wrong - effusion gives a dull drum and a flat type B tympanogram, not a peak at 0 daPa.
Wrong - discontinuity gives a hypermobile type Ad trace with high compliance.
Correct - stapes fixation gives conductive loss, a 2 kHz Carhart notch and a type As trace.
Wrong - tympanosclerotic plaques are visible on the drum, and her drums are normal.
Wrong - outer hair cell loss is sensorineural, with no air-bone gap.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old man woke this morning with a blocked, deaf right ear and loud tinnitus. There is no vertigo, pain or discharge. Otoscopy is normal on both sides. With a 512 Hz tuning fork, Rinne is positive in both ears and Weber lateralises to the left.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Nasal decongestant and autoinflation, review in 6 weeks
Softening drops and ear syringing of the right ear
Oral amoxicillin for presumed otitis media
Same-day ENT referral for PTA and oral steroids
Reassure and repeat tuning fork tests in a month
mcq.e: Rinne positive with **Weber lateralising to the better (left) ear** means a **right sensorineural loss**; a conductive loss would send Weber to the deaf ear. Sudden SNHL is an **otological emergency**: confirm with same-day PTA and start high-dose oral steroid (e.g. prednisolone 1 mg/kg, maximum 60 mg) as early as possible, then MRI IAM to exclude a retrocochlear cause. The trap is treating a 'blocked ear' as wax or Eustachian tube dysfunction.
w: Wrong - this treats Eustachian tube dysfunction, but the tuning forks show sensorineural loss.
Wrong - the canals are clear on otoscopy, and syringing does nothing for cochlear loss.
Wrong - the drums are normal, so there is no evidence of otitis media.
Correct - sudden SNHL needs same-day audiometry and early oral steroids.
Wrong - a month's delay loses the window in which steroids help recovery.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old girl had bilateral grommets inserted 6 months ago for glue ear. At review both ears are dry. Tympanometry of the right ear shows a flat trace with no identifiable peak and an ear canal volume of 2.4 ml; before surgery the same ear read 0.7 ml.
What is the best interpretation of the right tympanogram?
o: Middle ear effusion behind a blocked grommet
Grommet extruded into canal and blocked by wax
Eustachian tube dysfunction with negative pressure
Hypermobile drum from ossicular discontinuity
A patent grommet connecting canal and middle ear
mcq.e: A **type B** (flat) trace must be read with the **ECV**: **normal ECV = effusion**, **low ECV = wax or probe against the canal wall**, **high ECV = perforation or patent grommet**, because the probe now measures the canal plus the middle ear space. A jump from 0.7 to 2.4 ml with a dry ear means the grommet is open and working. Note: slide p98 describes type B as having normal ECV; type B is any flat trace, and the ECV tells you the cause.
w: Wrong - a blocked grommet with effusion gives a flat trace with a normal, not raised, ECV.
Wrong - wax blocking the canal gives a flat trace with a low ECV.
Wrong - Eustachian tube dysfunction gives a type C trace with a negative-pressure peak.
Wrong - discontinuity gives a type Ad trace with a tall peak, not a flat one.
Correct - a flat trace with a high ECV after grommet insertion means a patent grommet.

mcq.stem:
A 7-year-old boy has had a blocked left ear for 10 days after a cold, with no pain or fever. Otoscopy shows a retracted tympanic membrane with a prominent short process of the malleus and no fluid level. Left tympanometry: peak at −250 daPa, static compliance 0.6 ml, ECV 0.8 ml.
Which tympanogram type is this, and what does it indicate?
o: Type B, indicating middle ear effusion
Type As, indicating a stiff, fixed ossicular chain
Type C, indicating Eustachian tube dysfunction
Type Ad, indicating ossicular discontinuity
Type A, indicating a normal middle ear
mcq.e: Normal peak pressure is **+50 to −100 daPa** with compliance 0.3-1.7 ml. A peak shifted well into **negative pressure with normal compliance and ECV is type C**, meaning the middle ear is below atmospheric pressure because of **Eustachian tube dysfunction**, here after an upper respiratory infection. It may progress to effusion (type B) but usually resolves with watchful waiting or autoinflation.
w: Wrong - type B has no peak at all; this trace has a clear peak.
Wrong - type As peaks near 0 daPa with low compliance; here compliance is normal and the peak is negative.
Correct - a peak at −250 daPa with normal compliance and ECV is type C from Eustachian tube dysfunction.
Wrong - type Ad peaks near 0 daPa with very high compliance.
Wrong - type A peaks between +50 and −100 daPa; −250 daPa is outside that range.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old man was punched on the right side of the head 3 weeks ago and has had right-sided hearing loss since then. The tympanic membrane is intact, with no blood behind it. PTA: right AC 50 dB HL and BC 10 dB HL across frequencies. Right tympanometry: peak at 0 daPa, static compliance 3.0 ml, ECV 1.3 ml.
What is the most likely cause?
o: Dislocation at the incudostapedial joint
Haemotympanum from temporal bone fracture
Traumatic stapes footplate fixation
Traumatic perforation of the pars tensa
Eustachian tube oedema with negative pressure
mcq.e: **Type Ad**: normal peak pressure with **markedly raised compliance** (above 1.7 ml), meaning a **flaccid, hypermobile system**. With an intact drum and a large conductive loss (40 dB air-bone gap) after head trauma, this means **ossicular discontinuity**, most often at the incudostapedial joint or the long process of the incus. A thin, scarred drum can also give type Ad, but would not explain a 40 dB gap.
w: Correct - a hypermobile type Ad trace with a large conductive gap after trauma means ossicular discontinuity.
Wrong - haemotympanum fills the middle ear, giving a flat type B trace with normal ECV, and none is seen.
Wrong - fixation stiffens the system, giving type As (low compliance), not high compliance.
Wrong - the drum is intact; a perforation would give a flat trace with a high ECV.
Wrong - Eustachian tube dysfunction gives a negative-pressure type C peak.
